We apply our method to an actual dataset of rare flares detected by the Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor, focusing on three related phenomena: high-energy gamma-ray flares, short gamma-ray bursts, and X-ray outbursts. Our analysis reveals fluctuations in the relative timing of these phenomena, suggesting that the underlying physical processes may be influencing each other and potentially triggering rare flares.

This review explores the concept of hybrid quantum conductors that incorporate elements of BCS theory and the resonant valence bond theory, with a focus on the entangled Cooper pairs that play a crucial role in their operation. It encompasses a broad range of materials, including organic, inorganic, and hybrid materials, with particular emphasis on materials like $d$-transition metal oxides, $f$-transition metal compounds, and organic materials, as well as examples of exact models and realistic scenarios with inherent imperfections. Throughout the review, we delve into the fundamental aspects, recent advancements, and potential future directions in this field, with an emphasis on the impact of entangled Cooper pairs and the friction between quantum conduction and resistance.

The production of a precise, new isotope of germanium with mass number 70 via the combination of an algal system and an accelerator was achieved. This new isotope decays through a $\beta$-delayed three-body process into a specific state of oxygen with an excitation of 7.65 MeV and a nuclear structure that resembles nickel. Research indicates that a specific region around neutron number 40, has a distinct, resilient structure. Unlike nickel at this number, germanium exhibits a structure that is more symmetrical and rigid. A model based on cluster dynamics accurately predicts the probability of three-body distribution in the decay of this new isotope, taking into account the structures of the parent and daughter nuclei as well as their interaction at the time of decay. Data on the decay pattern match predictions from a nuclear many-body calculation, which suggests that the regions around neutron number 40 in both $\^{70}$Ge and $^{70}$O Ni exhibit a strong, central structure characterized by a compact, symmetrical arrangement of particles.

The development of a dual system combining the $B\\o$-IMS and Vienna-LMBCS detectors enabled precise measurement of highly radioactive, short-lived isotopes. Researchers utilized this setup to identify and study numerous novel isotopes and examine nuclear processes along the proton separation path. The focus was on measuring the properties of 64Co, 63Co, 62Co, and 61Co isotopes, which were detected as part of a 63Ni beam targeted at a thick silver foil. The produced Co isotopes were then analyzed as they emerged from the reaction, yielding significant insights into the underlying processes. Isotopes 64Co and 63Co were also identified and studied in an additional experiment utilizing the BoIMS detector in conjunction with a beam of 64Ni interacting with a nickel target.

We have developed a novel approach to representing U(1) gauge theories within the context of normalizing flows. This innovative method embeds the gauge symmetry into the flow itself, thereby maintaining a fixed Ward identity throughout the training process. As a result, any violations of unitarity resulting from conventional maximum likelihood optimization are avoided. We have successfully applied our technique to simulate both a simple pen-and-paper model and a more complex lattice scattering model. Our calculations have yielded reliable high-energy scattering data that aligns with the predicted asymptotic scaling behavior. Furthermore, we have observed unitarity throughout the entire scattering process.

This paper details a dataset developed for recognizing English addresses in images. The dataset is called ENADDR and consists of a collection of images, along with their corresponding annotations in a format suitable for training sequence-to-sequence neural networks. ENADDR is biased towards including only addresses that are properly formatted as per the United States Postal Service Code, which helps in recognizing poorly written addresses. ENADDR is particularly useful for training address validation models. ENADDR currently comprises 30,000 images, along with their annotations, and is available in public domain at https://github.com/google/ENADDR.

The cross-section for top quark production at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV has been measured in proton-antiproton collisions at the CERN LHC using the ATLAS experiment. The measurement was made with an integrated luminosity of 2.1 fb^-1} in events containing one charged particle and either two leptons or an energetic jet, in order to define and characterize the relevant signal and background processes. The measured cross-section, 232 ± 2 (stat.) ± 14 (sys.) nb, is in agreement with theoretical predictions from perturbative quantum chromodynamics and previous measurements at the same energy from the ATLAS and CMS experiments.

Developing database-driven DRL models using real databases is difficult and
expensive due to varying database contents that make training and updating models
time-consuming and costly. Even when successful, their effectiveness is severely
limited in practical scenarios such as: (1) significant drops in execution time
accuracy when database contents differ from those used in training, and (2) high
computational requirements for online prediction. To address these challenges, 
this paper proposes a novel framework that employs structural properties of SQL
queries and relational databases to learn offline. The method involves two key
components: (1) a graph generator module (GGM) that learns to map databases and
generate query graphs, and (2) a value predictor module (VP) responsible for
guessing missing value details. The proposed framework offers two significant
advantages: (1) high accuracy for a wide range of database contents, and (2)
online execution efficiency and improved accuracy by predicting more details. 
Experimental results show that this framework surpasses all competing offline
DRL-based methods in terms of execution accuracy and time efficiency, and even
matches some online DRL methods despite them outperforming all offline methods.

We examined angular clustering patterns of 0.15 < z < 2.5 galaxies from 0.25 < S$_{250\mu m}$ < 1000 in the LoTSS-HETDEX region. Considering the sensitivity and area over which the data were collected, this study pushed boundaries in two areas. The research used 1059 galaxies to analyze angular clustering at 1.2 < r < 16.5 Mpc/h and 16.5 < r < 40 Mpc/h. To verify accuracy, the results were compared to 11 sets of hydrodynamic simulations. These simulations aligned 71% to 82% with the $\Lambda$CDM cosmology as predicted. We applied a quadratic model to analyze the galaxy count correlation and found it to be the best fit. We calculated the galaxy bias and mass density overdensity at 1.2 < r < 16.5 Mpc/h and 16.5 < r < 40 Mpc/h. These values were $b=3.53\pm0.47$, $\Delta\rho_M/\bar{\rho}_M=2.15\pm0.45$ and $b=3.35\pm0.75$, $\Delta\rho_M/\bar{\rho}_M=1.85\pm0.75$ respectively. These outcomes align with the predictions from the majority of simulations.

We present an efficient algorithm for solving the rank-limited lasso problem in high dimensions, where we have a matrix of size $n \times p$ with $n$ representing samples and $p$ representing features. Our approach involves an adaptive sieving technique that reduces the dimensionality of the problem gradually. Firstly, we formulate a sequence of optimized problems with constrained ranks, where each iteration refines the solution by incorporating previously calculated estimates. Subsequently, we introduce a sieving procedure to selectively include or exclude columns from the matrix $\Phi$ and row vectors $Y$ in an iterative manner. This adaptive algorithm terminates prematurely once the solution converges with the imposed rank constraint. Notably, our method offers a significant runtime reduction compared to standard methods, particularly when dealing with large datasets containing numerous irrelevant features. Comprehensive numerical experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed algorithm, which outperforms conventional methods in terms of prediction accuracy, rank estimation, and computational speed. Moreover, we analytically prove the correctness and provide statistical guarantees for our adaptive algorithm.

We optimally determine the maximum possible entropy production in a closed system over time, utilizing a control technique known as optimal switching control. This builds upon our previous calculations of the lowest possible entropy production rate, which involved identifying the best temporal distribution of non-spontaneous work. Contrary to previous outcomes, a universal and optimal strategy for entropy production is found, which successfully captures the temporal aspect. A unique characteristic of this outcome is that it's based on the largest possible fluctuations in the system's energy variable. Uniqueness was achieved by incorporating a time-lag constraint into the problem.

As artificial intelligence continues to evolve, its applications are becoming integral to various industries and services, encompassing not only computational requirements but also a significant amount of electrical energy consumption. To thoroughly understand the environmental impact of AI, it is crucial to consider its entire lifecycle, encompassing development, deployment, and usage phases. This study conducts comprehensive assessments of three prevalent AI services - language translation, image recognition, and sentiment analysis - encompassing compute instances in data centers and edge deployments. These assessments encompass energy consumption, e-waste production, and greenhouse gas emissions. Findings indicate that sentiment analysis exhibits the highest environmental impact due to high data center energy consumption and substantial computing demands, whereas image recognition shows the highest e-waste production at 1.1 kg per user interaction result. Conversely, language translation exhibits relatively lower energy consumption and emissions of 0.06 kg CO2e and 0.0017 kWh-e per user interaction result, respectively. Nonetheless, it is essential to note that these values significantly depend on the specific configurations and locations of the AI services.

Current process monitoring techniques primarily focus on descriptive analyses, with only a few approaches designed to provide predictive recommendations to improve current processes. To address a lack of empirical validation for these methods, we aim to introduce a key reference model for evaluating and comparing proactive process monitoring techniques. We develop a framework to assess these methods through both theoretical and practical evaluations. We utilize this framework to test and compare four prescriptive process monitoring methods, revealing that a method grounded in causal graph models performs well across various scenarios, both in simulated and real-world processes.

This study introduces an error estimation technique for a coupled problem involving fluid mechanics and solid mechanics. The estimation relies on a dual-weighted residual method and a certified reliability technique. The estimation process involves dividing the computational domain into smaller regions, solving a corresponding variational problem in each area, and evaluating the error within each partition. The approach splits the estimation process into two parts: predicting a residual function and solving an auxiliary problem to obtain reliability terms. The prediction step uses an adaptive method to estimate the residual, and the second step solves a set of linear equations derived from the reliability term. The technique is implemented and tested on several coupled fluid-solid problems, including a moving boundary problem, a cavity flow with an embedded solid, and a steady-state flow with a solid attached. The numerical results show that the error estimates match the actual errors, and the technique provides reliable estimates for a wide range of parameters.

Graph packing problems have significant applications across various fields including network design and scheduling. To address these problems, researchers often employ techniques such as linear programming relaxations and randomized rounding algorithms. Obtaining tight bounds for such problems, especially those Involving vertex-disjoint paths, remains challenging due to the inherent complexity of the issues involved. In this research, we introduce a novel approach to derive tighter lower bounds for vertex-disjoint paths packing problems in graphs with specific structures. This research focuses on Eulerian graphs, for which the vertex-disjoint paths packing problem is equivalent to the halving problem. We employ a novel approach of convexifying the halving problem and applying continuous solutions to obtain lower bounds. Using this method, we derive improved lower bounds for the halting problem on Eulerian graphs and circle graphs. Furthermore, we explore the feasibility of converting the derived bounds into integer solutions, resulting in new record-low upper bounds for the 11- and 12-vertex classes in the halving problem.

We examine how complex social structures emerge from fundamental opinions and their interactions. Our model begins with one-dimensional opinions, representing extreme views at one end and moderate views at the other, similar to a temperature gradient. Agents with similar opinions form alliances. Over time, opinions become localized in distinct groups, comprising individuals with homogeneous views. These groups partition the opinion space, leading to permanent divisions, even when diverse perspectives are present. Our analysis reveals that extreme views exacerbate the formation of lasting social barriers, while moderate views delay the emergence of these barriers. Extremist perspectives accelerate the formation of a polarized social landscape, resulting in irrevocable divisions within the group.

We've investigated a two-dimensional black hole possessing scalar properties using the BPS equations from the $N=2$ supergravity model. The resulting black hole, characterized by two energy eigenvalues, displays both similar and distinct behaviors compared to holographic superconductors in certain aspects. Unlike its superconducting counterpart, this black hole fails to exhibit a second order phase transition, yet it does demonstrate a direct transition when a certain parameter is gradually increased from zero. Additionally, the black hole's scalar field displays a unique, asymmetrical profile in the presence of an external magnetic field.

The time gap between the completion of transcription and the generation of mature mRNA, taking into account processing events, can vary significantly across genes. This study examined processing events in mouse mRNAs exceeding 1 kb in length, analyzing delays ranging from several minutes to over an hour. Genes with extended delays were overrepresented among those involved in regulating cell growth, development, and tissue-specific expression. Notably, genes encoding ribosomal proteins exhibited the longest waiting periods, which correlated with their elevated levels of critical transcription factors. These findings imply that processing serves as a checkpoint Enabling adjustments to mRNA production based on factors such as alterations in ribosome requirements, alterations in metabolism, or changes in cell growth mode.

The evolution of the excitation energy in the 64Ni nucleus, specifically with respect to the neutron N = 40 subshell gap and the monopole interaction, shows a direct correlation. Using the 40Ca and 100Sn core models, researchers have investigated the properties of closed-core systems and calculated the excitation energies of the 64Ni ground band and proton particle excitations. In this study, the authors emphasize the significance of the monopole interaction in the structure and spectrum of 64Ni.

We're studying an SU(N) gauge theory that includes additional Weyl fermions, specifically Nf type I fermions in the fundamental representation and NF type II fermions in the adjoint representation. These type II fermions come in (N-1) flavor components. We've established that the resulting theory experiences a family of 2A N+1-1 anomalies for NF < N, (N-1)NF. We've demonstrated that these type II fermions generate a NF contribution to the theta-angle rotation parameter in the SU(N) anomaly polynomial, A(Nf, NF; π). We've also found that the type II fermions yield an (N-1)NF correction to the 2A N+1-1 term. We've verified our findings by introducing a local NF counterterm to the action while verifying its invariance under the SU(N)Weyl group through a mathematical analysis.

Consider two group codes, C and D, with the property that D is D^⊥, transposed. This implies an equivalence relationship between codes C and D based on a specific homomorphism defined between the abelian groups, <C|K/ZZ> and <D|K/ZZ>. This paper explores the extent of this equivalence phenomenon in the context of group codes. It begins by establishing the principle that if code C can be expressed as a quotient of free abelian groups a and b, then its dual code, D, will have an abelian structure in terms of the group modulo the product of a and b. Examples illustrating the equivalence phenomenon are provided for specific cases of group codes, including toroidal codes, which are a particular type of group code, and Gelfand--Goresky--MacPherson (GGM) codes. Additionally, the paper examines the properties of pre-DuPré groups and demonstrates that a group code with the property that its dual code, D, is isomorphically related to a p-median code, with p a prime number, cannot achieve the p-median code's maximum capacity, denoted as Gamma_p.

Bucket Elimination is a method of efficient inference and optimization in graphical models. It works by dividing the model into self-contained components, allowing for efficient computation of most efficient problem solutions. However, the standard Bucket Elimination method can get stuck in infinite loops on models with cyclic structures. This paper presents a novel, on-the-fly bucket creation approach that avoids the division of the model into distinct components at the beginning. Instead, the algorithm dynamically creates buckets as needed based on elimination results. Moreover, the paper introduces a criterion for determining whether a bucket can be safely eliminated without restarting the process. This allows the algorithm to avoid getting stuck in infinite loops even in the presence of models with cyclic patterns. Experimental findings confirm that the on-the-fly bucket creation method outperforms alternative approaches and yields faster run times.

The ability to recognize objects that have fallen to the ground is essential for creating and sustaining a relationship between a robot and its environment. This is particularly true for a robot's learning and navigation tasks, where it must integrate visual and kinesthetic sensory information to identify objects that have dropped. In this paper, we present our approach to recognizing objects that have fallen to the ground using a pre-trained Inception network, and we demonstrate the efficacy of our method through a simulation in a 2D environment in which a learned agent navigates and accumulates visual, kinesthetic, and proprioceptive sensory experiences. As a result of using an Inception network to consolidate sensory experiences, our navigation tests show a notable improvement of 15% to 20% in object recognition speed and accuracy compared to a method that uses a pre-trained Convolutional Neural Network. Additionally, our results indicate that incorporating kinesthetic and proprioceptive sensory experiences enhances object recognition both speed and accuracy by 5% to 10%.

We investigate the application of scaling theory to the volume and shear modulus of particulate materials undergoing jamming transitions. The study combines numerical simulations with one-dimensional and three-dimensional models, where different theoretical frameworks are employed for jamming transitions occurring via isotropic or shear processes. Specifically, for isotropic jamming, we find evidence supporting a scaling law with a critical exponent of 1.4, although this value disagree with earlier work that suggested a value of 1. This discrepancy prompted a re-examination of the theoretical framework for shear jamming, where we discovered a scaling law with a critical exponent of 3/5 in one dimension and 1.5 in three dimensions. Despite initial expectations to the contrary, our results indicate that the exponents for shear and isotropic jamming are distinct. Moreover, we observed exponents for shear jamming that differ between 1-dimensional and 3-dimensional models.

This research introduces a novel AR model designed to capture short-term dynamics in time series data. Specifically, the study focuses on simulating daily electricity demand in Germany and Italy from 2020 to 2021. By combining the MS(2)-AR(4) model with an ETS component for longer-term trends, the work demonstrates that this multi-scale approach outperforms a standard autoregressive model in capturing the intricate dynamics of electricity demand.

Government professionals and officials require up-to-to-date knowledge of current issues and policies to make informed decisions. As a primary source of information, search engines like Google have become an essential tool for many public sector workers. However, recent studies have demonstrated that Google's algorithm is biased, with search results for specific terms and phrases being influenced by factors such as location, connection IP, and past search history. These biases can compromise decision-making and the credibility of public sector professionals by providing inaccurate or incomplete information. To address this, we have developed a study which aims to provide public sector organizations with practical guidance and insights on how these biases affect Web search results. Our research focuses on algorithmic biases in Google's search outcomes related to job applicants, with specific emphasis on gender and age considerations. We also examine the potential implications of these biases for public sector recruitment and suggest strategies for mitigating their effects.

Our previous research introduced ProSyn, a program synthesis framework that uses
a learning-based approach to identify relevant sections within a code template.
This study builds upon ProSyn by enhancing the program synthesis module and
assessing its enhanced version, ProSyn+, which employs a more sophisticated
identification method of code sections. Experiments were conducted using a
modified version of the Grammer-Vita dataset, with both a code-generated
dataset and a dataset of natural language descriptions of code functions.
Results from a 100-trial synthesis show that ProSyn+ can synthesize programs in
as little as 0.05 seconds, with an average of 15.52 seconds, indicating a
significant improvement over the original ProSyn. Furthermore, 89% of the
synthesized programs in the code-generated dataset and 80% in the description
dataset compiled successfully with no errors, with 94% and 83% respectively
passing a basic test of functionality in Java.

To help mitigate climate change, it's crucial to develop reduced-order models of the Earth's climate system that can accurately capture its essential features and variability. These models typically rely on linear multi-scale methods that separate the into small and large scales, averaging the latter to represent its dominant behavior. However, this approach can be problematic if the primary variability arises from the small scales. Instead, we propose a novel approach based on linear Flato methods that identifies and dissects the climate system into its cohesive and disintegrative components. This reduction process yields an efficient, computationally integral model that integrates the boundaries between these categories, preserving the original system's dynamics. Our method surpasses conventional reduction techniques in terms of accuracy and scalability, as illustrated by its application to a simplified global climate model and an atmospheric GCM.

The upcoming LSST is anticipated to yield substantial data, encompassing around 900,000 potential kilonova events, although its ability to capture detailed infrared spectra using its Eu:Yb laser guide star may be limited to 10-20% of these events. However, the JWST, equipped with the Mid-Infrared Instrument, has the capability to observe a broader range of these events, possibly up to 30, 000-40, 000 kilonovae per year in its initial one and a half years of operation. By taking narrower fields, JWST could observe a larger portion, up to 50-60% of kilonovae, and this would significantly benefit the understanding of electron custody in kilonovae, especially those with higher blue colors.

X-ray beam delivery in radiation oncology can be marred by variations in tumor position, image uncertainty, and inconsistent organ boundaries in follow-up imaging. To address these issues and ensure precise tumor coverage, adaptive X-ray beam modulation during treatment is necessary. Real-time, high-speed tracking of tumor position via X-rays is crucial but difficult to achieve solely using X-rays. To overcome this limitation, we propose using spinal markers and position sensors to estimate tumor position, utilizing X-ray flux measurements to refine the estimate when available. To modulate adaptive X-ray beams, we employ a two-stage process: first, generating a treatment plan through fluence optimization, and then adjusting the beam shape to match the optimized fluence. To efficiently calculate the optimized fluence, we use an iterative convex optimization method, and to quickly adjust the beam shape in real-time, we employ a look-up table-based approach. To test our proposed method, we used synthetic tumor trajectories and simulated noisy fluence measurements, forming the basis of a practical algorithm to calculate optimal fluences and an experimental system for real-time beam shape adjustment. Results from a comprehensive clinical study with an experienced radiation oncologist showed a significant reduction in the amount of X-ray beam. To test our proposed method in the absence of X-ray flux measurements, we employed spinal marker and sensor position measurements as surrogate signals, yielding comparable results to flux-based optimization. To further improve our method, we plan to incorporate flux measurements, implement it on a real-time, programmable system

In compositional data analysis, it's typical to apply Aitchison's logratio transformation to the components of data vectors. The main advantage of this transformation is that it preserves the geometry of the composition space. However, finding a suitable multivariate kernel for likelihood estimation in high-dimensional data is challenging due to the limited number of data observations available for reliable estimation. A novel, enhanced multivariate logratio kernel is developed that incorporates a uniform prior distribution over the composition space, taking into account the matrix determinant and the spread of the components. This new kernel, known as the Dirichlet-uniform (DU) kernel, utilizes the multivariate gamma function to unify various scalar operators and achieve a constant value for the kernel value at the origin. Results demonstrate that this DU kernel outperforms other methods such as the symmetric squared Euclidean kernel, the chi-square kernel, and the maximum likelihood estimators-based logratio kernel in terms of the predictive loss for several real-world high-dimensional data sets.

The core accretion model's prediction that most gas giant planets should have evolved into hot Jupiters is not supported by observations, as these planets make up only a small fraction of all gas giant planets.  To better understand how planets develop according to this model, researchers simulated a large number of planet formations and tracked their movements, applying these simulations to explain the diversity in sizes of planets observed.  In contrast to previous predictions, the observed distribution of exoplanets does not favor the core accretion theory regarding runaway gas accretion; instead, most planets are thought to be super-Jupiters that are then reduced in size.  To resolve the discrepancy between the core accretation model's predictions and observations, another theory, the streaming instability, was explored.  In this theory, the presence of small particles in protoplanetary disks can cause the coagensation of solid matter, allowing for the rapid growth of planetary cores.  Although the theory can account for the diversity in planetary sizes, issues remain as to whether the cores can prevent gas accretion and whether the theory's predictions align with observations of protoplanetary disks.

Recent examples of dynamic memory in models, such as LIM and LIM-E, have shown potential in tracking unobserved states and improving predictions from partial observations. However, these models rely on the presence of latent variables to function effectively, which poses a problem for their application in systems that rely on end-to-end training, such as generative modeling and reinforcement learning. The proposed architecture, MHM, offers a alternative solution to dynamic memory by utilizing a hierarchical structure to represent temporal relationships and improve performance on tasks such as time-series forecasting, activity tracking, and generative modeling, all without the need for latent variables.

We present a theoretical model in which a discrete symmetry known as $Z_3$ isolates two distinct sectors: one consisting of the fundamental Standard Model fields, and another comprising a dark matter candidate $S$, a scalar field $A$, and a fermion $\chi$. The sectors are connected through the mediation of a scalar $A$ that transmits weakly to the dark matter fields. Our model contains two types of dark matter interactions, defined by the mass ratio of the scalar mediator $A$ to the dark matter candidate $S$. If the mediator $A$ is heavier than the dark matter $S$, its relevant parameter space is compatible with Faree's bounds, offering a range for the mediator coupling $0.0031-\ 0.25$. Furthermore, we investigated the model's capacity to explain the Galactic 125 GeV excess observed by the AMS-01 experiment, discovering parameter combinations that align with the observed spectrum while meeting Faree's bounds. Conversely, if the mediator $A$ is lighter than the dark matter $S$, the interaction is strongly suppressed by the dark matter mass, fulfilling Faree's bounds with a mediator coupling between 0.00031 and 0.0031. In this scenario, we examined the model's potential to account for the Galactic 125 GeV excess and its failure to do so, given the dark matter's cross-section is two orders of magnitude lower than required. Lastly, we explored the model's ability to explain the observed

Research on cognitive batteries, particularly the CogAT battery, has shown that
even basic tasks are challenging for machines. Existing data sets often present
tasks in a straightforward, standardized manner, but a more nuanced approach
is needed to mimic human cognition more effectively. To address this, we have
developed Mod-Cog, a novel cognitive multi-task data set that offers a more
complex and diverse range of tasks within a modular design. Each task within
the data set is designed to build upon a basic Athanassiou task or to compete
with an equivalent basic task, allowing for both general and specialized AI
models to be evaluated. The comprehensive data set includes 289,917 initial
problems, 25,000 additional problems, and 1,000 instructional tasks, along with
a custom-designed search algorithm and web interface for seamless problem
presentation and scoring. We have also utilized the data set to investigate the
performance of both neural and symbolic AI models, with the results indicating
that even the most advanced neural models struggle with many of the data set's
tasks, creating opportunities for new research and the development of more
advanced AI models.

This paper delves into the geometric aspects of nilpotent algebras, examining how their properties change as a given dimension changes. Specifically, we're looking at varieties of nilpotent algebras of step $r$, comprised of elements of a fixed dimension $n$. These varieties are defined using a finite set of equations, based on the bracket operation, which can be broken down into simpler polynomial inequalities. By analyzing the structure of these polynomials, we're able to gain insights into the nature of the resulting algebraic varieties, including their components, dimension, and relationships. We're also looking at subspace arrangements, which give rise to families of non-nilpotent algebras, and nilpotent algebras over fields of positive characteristic, exploring their unique properties and geometric characteristics.

Large-scale jets originating from Active Galactic Nuclei, which stretch out into the surrounding space, seem to be inscribed on the cosmos canvas. A prominent theory suggests that inverse Compton interaction between high-speed electrons and cosmic microwave background photons is responsible for the observed radiation. However, it is essential to address a fundamental issue with inverse Compton scattering, namely its inability to generate synchrotron radiation at the same intensity level. A new model proposes an alternative explanation for the origin of large-scale jets, suggesting that the electrons in the jets become cold in low-density regions due to a decrease in energy loss rate, thereby enabling the reversal of energy flux and intensity to match observational data. Moreover, this model is compatible with the findings of supermassive black hole growth rates and provides a plausible mechanism for the observed kiloparsec-scale radio emission.

We examine the analytical expansion of the Schwarzschild metric in the near-non-relativistic limit. This limit is useful for examining phenomena at non-relativistic speeds and large distances from the source, and it can be applied to a more general case of any metric. We also discuss how this approach might be used to identify non-relativistic characteristics in gravitational systems where relativistic effects are present.

A multi-scale image registration technique, SIFT-CPD, is introduced to align medical images with varying intensity contrast and local abnormalities. This method utilizes a robust scale-invariant feature detection algorithm and a compact pattern description framework for registration. To improve the technique's computational efficiency, a coarse-to-fine approach is implemented, combining image up-sampling and descent iterations. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of SIFT-CPD in registering MRI scans of the brain, bone, and abdomen with contrast agents, as well as registering non-contrast to contrast-enhanced images. A comprehensive evaluation framework, including metric analysis and registration performance assessment, supports the use of SIFT-CPD. Additionally, the implementation of this method, along with associated data and software, is made available to the public for future development.

We have identified a unique binary star system, SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, which is known for displaying an unusual eclipse that can be attributed to both eclipsing detached double-degenerate binaries. This remarkable phenomenon is likely the result of two white dwarfs orbiting closer towards the end of their natural lifespan, causing their surfaces to continuously collide and lead to the disappearance of their characteristic eclipse signatures over time. This discovery offers a rare opportunity to study the final stages of binary star evolution through theoretical analysis and by comparing it to real-world observations of this system and its counterparts, which is expected to provide valuable insights into the processes that lead to the formation of these double-degenerate binaries.

In recent years, the development of various neural network architectures has disparities in their underlying principles and multiple conflicting recommendations have emerged, making it challenging for researchers and engineers to choose an optimal architecture for a particular task. In an effort to simplify the design of neural networks, this paper introduces the UOT-pooling (UOP) framework, which unifies distinct network architectures and effectively merges their benefits. The proposed UOP framework is based on a novel filtering mechanism and is capable of merging networks at both module and pool levels. The framework's applicability and effectiveness are demonstrated through experiments in multiple image classificationscenarios, where it consistently outperforms popular network architectures, including ResNet, MobileNet, and EfficientNet.

We analyzed the distribution of polar alignment in a sample of 91 active galactic nuclei from the 16th Sloan Digital Sky Survey release. The sample is divided into three subgroups: low-velocity type 1 Seyfert nuclei, high-velocity type 1 quasars, and type 2 Seyfert nuclei. For the first time, we have studied the distribution of polar alignment in a significant sample of type 2 active galactic nuclei using a sophisticated technique that considers the light from the nucleus and surrounding disk. Unlike type 1 nuclei, which align in a uniform direction, and type 2 nuclei, whose alignment distribution differs, we discovered that type 2 Seyfert nuclei exhibit characteristics similar to type 1 Seyfert nuclei in spiral host galaxies. Additionally, while type 2 Seyfert nuclei exhibit various orientation distributions based on host galaxy type, torus subtypes, and hard X-ray luminosity, we did not find a significant difference in polar alignment of type 2 Seyfert nuclei compared to type 1 Seyfert nuclei.

In this study, we examine a general Riemann surface's properties based on its Gauss map. Specifically, we focus on pointwise 1-type Gauss maps for flat general rotation surfaces. First, we establish that these maps are characterized by a unique property: they are concyclic with the preimage of each point. We then demonstrate that for a point off the axis, it is possible to reconstruct the surface up to isometry using the preimage of that point and its tangent plane. Additionally, we investigate the integral geometry of 1-type Gauss maps for flat general surfaces of negative curvature.

Reconstructing 3D scenes from multiple images is a more challenging task
than using single images to categorize objects, but the skills learned in the
process are equally applicable to object recognition tasks. To demonstrate this
potential, we developed a novel self-supervised method for 3D scene
reconstruction that serves as a pre-training framework. The method employs
geometric information to force agreement across multiple views of a scene,
relying on sophisticated 3D geometric constraints rather than simple spatial
arrangements. The introduction of an innovative optimization procedure for 3D
point cloud registration allows our approach to outperform other state-of-the-art
techniques in terms of 3D reconstruction accuracy, even when the method is
subsequently fine-tuned using supervised learning. Furthermore, we observed
that our pre-training method leads to significant improvements in object
recognition within the SUN3D dataset, even when object-level geometric
information is not available.

Developing data-driven time-series models from scratch is complicated by the absence of adequate training data, hindering innovation in the field. To address this challenge, we present TCube, a novel time-series dataset with comprehensive annotations that facilitates automated data preparation for the task. TCube incorporates a range of sophisticated time-series processing techniques, including a linear model predictor that identifies redundant data patterns and removes them from the training process. The dataset features 1,916,804 minutes of annotated flight data, spanning 2,882 seconds, from 468 vehicles, making it the largest dataset of its kind. To assess the efficacy of TCube, we conducted six time-series analysis challenges, involving 33 teams from 57 educational institutions, who achieved notable advancements in the field. The full details of our dataset and analysis can be accessed at https://tcube.aero/.

The most precise analyses of rare decays, specifically $B^0_s\to\mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0\to\mu^+\mu^-$, have been conducted using proton-proton collision data, collected at LHCb by 2011-2016, and totaling 9 $ {\rm fb}^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. The rates of these decays were measured against two theoretical models for their occurrence, one being the Standard Model of particle physics and the other describing possible effects of new physics due to right-handed currents. When compared to previous studies, these rates revealed no significant deviations from the Standard Model predictions. Calculations of observables in these decays, particularly $\mathcal{B}(B^0\to\mu^+\mu^-)$ and $C_7^{\rm NP}$, were also performed, indicating that the data on these decays, as analyzed, do not support the possibility of new physics affecting these processes at the level of 0.1% to 0.3%. Furthermore, the data on $C_7^{\rm NP}$ allowed for limits to be set on how large this theoretical parameter could be, with its unit being restricted to less than $8\cdot10^{-3}$ in the context of right-handed current effects.

We investigate the Ising model on Cayley trees represented by group elements, utilizing various group representations in the analysis. The study moves beyond the traditional approach of examining a single group representation, instead exploring both the canonical trigonometric algebra and arbitrary group representations. The resulting thermodynamic equations are scrutinized in detail to uncover both general and specific outcomes, such as the existence of phase transitions and free energy calculations, all within the context of group representation theory.

The focus of this research is the study of solutions to hyperbolic equations, specifically those with metric perturbations that are not smooth. We are interested in understanding how certain properties of the metric affect the regularity of solutions. We show that if the metric has a singularity, but is otherwise smooth outside a compact set, then the solutions to these equations will also have singularities, regardless of the large data limits. This contrasts with the behavior of solutions when the metric is smooth, where the singularities are confined to a compact set. We also explore the consequences of allowing non-smooth data, resulting in solutions with singular behavior.

This research explores an effective method for enhancing Japanese word segmentation using the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network. LSTM is commonly applied in handling language sequences with long-term memory issues, but it has not been extensively utilized in Japanese word segmentation tasks. To improve accuracy, a new approach involves combining LSTM with a Char-CNN character-level model that utilizes character features. This strategy involves using a Char-CNN to extract essential character features, which are then integrated with LSTM for sentence feature extraction. Thereafter, a Char-CNN model is used to project the extracted features onto a fixed vector space for classification. This research introduces a novel algorithm, which demonstrates superior performance on the NiHAGAN dataset compared to existing methods such as the Bi-LSTM and Char-CNN models.

Our proposal focuses on utilizing information from Stack Overflow's largest code repository to assist programmers in identifying popular external resources that could improve their productivity. By analyzing the site's metadata, we discovered that most valuable resources are frequently re-shared on the platform. To maximize benefits, we centered on extracting useful parameters from successful queries. Our analysis revealed that MATLAB and Python are the two dominant programming languages contributing to the site's knowledge base. Notably, parameters associated with these programming languages account for a substantial majority of all parameters. Ultimately, our research aims to enhance the site's value by promoting the utilization of its collected resources, thereby streamlining developers' workflows and increasing their productivity with a streamlined toolset.

About 50% of galaxies exhibit similar or higher central density in their rotation curves compared to their distant parts. Additionally, the diversity of galaxy rotation curves is surprising, given that they cover a broad range, from lookalike to upside-down shapes. Currently, the most accepted theory is the cusp-core theory, proposing that removing energy from the center of a galaxy's dark matter halo can transform a cusp-shaped density distribution to a core-like flatter distribution. Given that about 50% of galaxies are characterized by either cusp or core profiles, it's essential to distinguish whether dark matter or baryonic matter is primarily responsible for a galaxy's rotation curve. We present a new numerical model, IsoCore, designed to simulate a smooth isothermal core within a dark matter halo, surrounded by an unequal mass of baryonic matter. IsoCore is utilized to model 12 real galaxies with various rotation curves, employing an optimization algorithm that adjusts a range of physical parameters while minimizing discrepancies between simulated and observed rotation curves. The results show that IsoCore successfully reproduces a wide range of galaxy rotation curves, revealing a strong correlation between a galaxy's core radius and isothermal core radius, as well as its overall dark matter distribution.

Despite widespread agreement on the need for urgent climate action, progress has been slow. People's perceptions of their personal values and priorities do shift in response to learning about climate change, but often result in feelings of inadequacy and inaction. This study explores how people's awareness of their personal values and priorities in relation to climate change can be supported, with a goal of motivating climate action. A value-based framework has been established, with an integrated system that draws from cognitive science and decision theory, designed to accommodate diverse human values. Through a process called gradual value-based guidance, this system helps individuals prioritize actions in line with their personal values, with an option to update their values if desired. Early testing with a small group of people demonstrated improvement in their motivation to take climate action, with an approach that respects their autonomy and agency.

This paper presents a new task called Symptom Extraction, where doctors need to identify relevant information from unstructured medical notes to create a patient's clinical record. We've developed a novel approach to tackle this challenge by combining data augmentation and domain generalization techniques to improve neural machine translation performance. Our method uses multiple parallel datasets to train a translator that can generalize effectively even with minimal data, enhancing its robustness and translation quality significantly. We achieved impressive results in our experiments, outperforming traditional medical approaches and neural translation methods.

Autonomous vehicles operate effectively in observable conditions, but face challenges when surroundings change or objects appear/disappear. A combination of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and deep convolutional neural networks (DCNN) can capture driving patterns and adapt to unexpected scenarios. This study compares various RNN architectures, including vanilla RNN, GRU, and LSTM, to determine their effectiveness in autonomous driving applications. By evaluating the performance of different RNNs using metrics such as lane change error and root mean square deviation, the results reveal that LSTM-RNN surpasses vanilla RNN and GRU performance in partially observable scenarios. Furthermore, the integration of DCNN and LSTM-RNN significantly improves the evaluation metrics, demonstrating the importance of both components in autonomous driving systems.

Recent advancements in artificial neural networks have led to accurate data interpretation, yet their complex nature renders them computationally costly and impractically costly to train. In response, we present a straightforward, general-purpose classifier based on a single-layer perceptron with weighted sum of normalized features. We demonstrate that this model can consistently match the accuracy of traditional artificial neural networks while requiring significantly fewer computational resources, essentially zero power consumption. Additionally, our system excels in resource-constrained environments such as embedded devices, IoT, mobile devices, robotics, autonomous vehicles, and similar applications. A publicly accessible repository containing the code and datasets is available at https://github.com/JT-Lee14/NormalPerceptron.

In this research, we investigate the state equation of spin-polarized strange quark matter under the influence of a strong magnetic field within the framework of the bag model. Our calculations take into account the effects of the bag constant and quark masses. Furthermore, we derive the formula for the energy density of spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field. Our findings demonstrate that the magnetic field has a significant impact on the state equation of spin-polarized strange quark matter, and its behavior varies substantially according to different values of the bag constant and quark masses.

Personal devices are now capable of performing complex computational tasks like object detection, but such operations often require significant processing power and can strain device resources. Using cloud-based services like Google Cloud can expedite these processes, but this approach can be costly. Investigating an alternative, Pando, an open-source auto-tuning tool for computer vision tasks, was evaluated on a cluster of 48 personal devices. Comparing Pando's results with those from Google Cloud showed that Pando's speeds were just 8% slower while using personal devices' processing power was 18% less than that of Google Cloud, thus demonstrating a cost-effective, self-sustaining, and high-performance computing system.

This study presents an adaptive technique for extracting eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix, leveraging randomized methods and progressive submatrix extraction. The proposed adaptive strategy efficiently identifies eigenvalues outside the desired spectral range, where traditional approaches would require substantial computation. By integrating these adaptations into the Lanczos algorithm, we develop an enhanced iterative method for approximate eigenvalue computation. Experimental results demonstrate that this adaptive technique successfully accelerates eigenvalue estimation for matrices of varying sizes and types.

We examine bittable sets for the beta-transformation with non-integer base b greater than 2. Specifically, we identify the survivor sets for this transformation, establishing their relationship to badly approximable numbers in base b and showing these sets comprise those numbers with specific binary expansion properties. Moreover, we establish the connection between bittable sets for the associated interval exchange transformation and those for the beta-transformation. We also explore bittable sets for a broader class of transformations, defined by a non-integer base b and a non-zero rational slope α, but with limitations on their interval partitioning, known as the standard angle condition. We analyze the survivor sets for these transformations, revealing their connection to badly approximable numbers in base b and α. We also establish the connection between bittable sets for the standard angle condition and those for the beta2-transformation, which does not satisfy this condition.

In CONTOUR, an innovative lattice gauge theory software tool, we simulate $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theories in the fundamental representation to investigate SU(N$_{F}$) chiral symmetry breaking as a result of the influence of quark bilinears. Additionally, we have introduced a novel technique to optimize the overlap operator and effectively enhance the signal in relevant correlation functions. Our development is bolstered by an intuitive user interface, making it user-friendly for both experienced and novice researchers.

Real-world datasets often suffer from issues of confounding, where characteristics affecting the target variable are not independent of each other. In such cases, relying solely on model predictions can be misleading, as it fails to account for these interdependencies. We introduce a novel technique, Disentangled Attribution Curves, for uncovering hidden patterns in the absence of a control group, demonstrated through analysis of the bike-sharing dataset. This method combines partial dependence plots with causal discovery strategies to reveal the disentangled effects of each attribute on the target variable, while accounting for the contributions of all other attributes.

Federated learning allows for the collaborative training of machine learning models, avoiding the need to transfer sensitive data. Despite this, previous methods have shown limitations in maintaining privacy and overcoming data heterogeneity. We introduce a groundbreaking approach that surpasses current standards in both privacy and performance. Our method incorporates a novel, efficient learning algorithm and a robust loss double-blind technique. We theoretically prove that this approach achieves the highest possible accuracy under optimal conditions. Moreover, we demonstrate the superior performance of our method over state-of-the-art baselines in scenarios involving private, non-private, heterogeneous, and non-heterogeneous data settings.

This document outlines a proposed solution for evaluating drivers on microcontroller hardware, featuring a web-based interface that allows users to write and compile driver code, as well as run it on a connected microcontroller, all from a browser. The solution involves a user-friendly web interface that will serve as the front-end, an LLVM-based toolchain for compilation, a web server running LLVM and a microcontroller driver to facilitate communication between the web interface and the microcontroller, as well as a device running this evaluation tool that will serve as the back-end.

System filters play a vital role in protecting applications from malicious activities, including unauthorized system calls. Current filters, however, primarily focus on applications written in C and other low-level languages. This paper introduces Timeloops, an advanced system call filtering framework designed for high-level languages such as Java, Python, and Ruby. Timeloops develops detailed system call timelines for each application, enabling precise control over system activity. By integrating with existing frameworks, Timeloops can block suspicious system calls in interpreted languages, including PHP. Our evaluation demonstrates that Timeloops can efficiently limit unwanted system calls while maintaining only minimal performance overhead.

Due to the inherent complexity of high-dimensional biologically driven data found in single-cell RNA sequencing, developing robust and interpretable models has become a significant challenge. As a result, the data is often simplified by being transformed into lower-dimensional spaces. Our research centers around understanding how the data's structure changes when reduced from its native space to a specific space called the product space, where individual features' product dimensions are included. The results show that the product space offers substantial improvements in classification accuracy for scRNA-seq data across various dimensions, achieving over 30% performance gain compared to traditional Euclidean spaces for low-dimensional spaces. Through the analysis of crucial network topological characteristics and critical data points, our method's high accuracy in the product space is explained. The novel approach we developed demonstrates potential applications in the challenging and essential tasks of visualizing and understanding scRNA-seq data.

In the vicinity of a supermassive black hole, the distribution of stars within its influence is deemed to be in a steady state. A key concept in this framework is the mass function of stars, which is a steady-state condition along with the number distribution of stars in the vicinity of the black hole. Previous research assumed a mass function based on a specific stellar mass spectrum and derived the resulting distribution of stars in the vicinity of the black hole. Contrary to expectations, this distribution is not uniform; rather, there are areas around the direct radial path that contain a higher concentration of stars. A statistical analysis revealed that a large majority of these'mass function' predictions align with existing observational data. Furthermore, the resulting data show that the scattering cross-section of stars in the vicinity of a supermassive black hole is significantly influenced by the mass function of these stars. Specifically, this cross-section is diminished when the mass function includes a substantial population of low-mass stars, a phenomenon that has been observed in certain galaxies.

This work centers around stochastic Model Predictive Control (SMPC) used for navigating uncertain systems with constraints. We introduce an approach that generates a control strategy through reinforcement learning to mitigate variability in stochastic systems. We show that RL-SMPControl, which employs a risk-averse policy, reduces variability compared to conventional MPC in risk-neutral systems, with the trade-off coming at the expense of increased constraint violation. We further investigate the structural properties of risk-averse policies and demonstrate that, under certain conditions, a more risk-averse approach leads to significantly reduced variability.

This research explores the application of compressive sensing techniques to ICA (independent component analysis) algorithms, introducing two innovative methods in the process. Our first approach combines compressive sensing and ICA into a single unified algorithm, while our second method leverages a pre-trained CS module in conjunction with standard ICA. Both of these schemes yield significant reductions in memory requirements, with our first method boasting a compressed memory footprint of $O(N)$ and the second method achieving a compressed memory footprint of $O(N^2)$. For evaluation, we utilize the SMOP algorithm as our base CS module, driven by neg-entropy optimization. Our results indicate that these compressive ICA algorithms exhibit negligible performance disparities from $50\%$ to $10\%$ in terms of accuracy, while offering substantial memory efficiency improvements.

This work extends the voter model to include competition between two species, with each species having a chance to change their vote with decreasing probability, creating an asymmetric noisy voter model. Mathematically, this model can be represented by a probability measure governing the states of a lattice network, where each node represents a species, with mechanisms governing species change and death driving the system towards various equilibrium states. Notably, this model exhibits a rich phase diagram, with multiple fixed points and periodic as well as chaotic patterns emerging from complex interactions between the two species.

We analyze von Neumann algebras generated by bounded, semi-finite weights on cones of gauge invariant operators for toric code models and an extended version of the Poincaré algebra. For these specific instances, the generated local algebras correspond to von Neumann factors of type $II$. We extend our study to a broader class of gauge invariant perturbations, demonstrating that the associated local algebras remain closed under strong operator approximation. Consequently, the maximal abelian subalgebras supporting ground states are continuous under perturbation and thus invariant under approximate unit limits, maintaining their structural integrity.

We experimentally examine the influence of a coherent feedback circuit on two-spade interactions within superconducting qubits, observing that coherent feedback enhances entanglement's resistance to heat-induced degradation. Furthermore, the area of applicability for feedback improvement is precisely defined by our experimental outcomes, constraints imposed by temperature and detection uncertainty. Notably, the interaction mediated by a coherent feedback loop serves as an exemplary model for the design of robust many-qubit algorithms in the near-term quantum device era.

We have calculated one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for massless gluons and massless quarks to third-order in QCD. These operators will be utilized in developing third-order massless QCD corrections to multi-jet production processes via parton splitting fragmentation functions.

Greenberg's strong approximation theorem for quasi-characters can be rephrased in terms of a particular set of equations involving polynomials with coefficients from the ring $R$. This set is in compliance with a second set of equations that arise from the coefficients of other polynomials, also in $R$. When $R$ is a one-dimensional local ring, this formulation connects to Weil's work on the product of polynomials mod $p$. If $R$ is the ring of integers in a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}_p$, the relationship becomes evident after standard reformulations. However, the presentation offered here diverges slightly from these standard forms, instead highlighting the interplay between the arithmetic of $R$ and the geometric properties of affine spaces over the field ${\bf k}_R$ with residue field ${\bf k}_R$.

This paper outlines a citizen science project aimed at learning about sundials across Indonesia through a mobile game. The increasing dissemination of smart devices has enabled individuals to easily access and utilize various technologies, including geolocation capabilities, and has potentially turned every mobile device into a tool for participating in scientific research. By building on this opportunity, we developed an innovative approach that converts the process of observing and recording sundials into an engaging and interactive experience for the general public. Our goal is to leverage the collective power of non-experts to document and contribute to the study of sundials across Indonesia.

In a zero-pairing DED2D game where players compete for discounted data and energy bundles, we propose the TFIET (Two-Flow-Interference-by-Error-and-Timing) strategy. It operates in two modes: at the data level, using a stochastic process similar to TSEI, and at the energy level, using a timing-based interference model. This strategy allows us to derive a compact expression for the TFIET policy, and analyze its performance in terms of interference, timing, and data accuracy. Additionally, we investigate the TFIET performance in a DED2D environment with multiple users.

The COVID-19 pandemic has led to a significant increase in remote work, forcing organizations to adapt their operations by implementing automated solutions for their operations. Research laboratories were no exception, with many experimenting with fully automated experimental setups that can be controlled remotely. To address the corresponding communications challenges, researchers have developed a range of solutions, including wireless sensor networks, remote control systems, and automated software tools. To successfully experiment and collect data, these setups require precise configuration and synchronization, which poses a major problem. Current automation efforts primarily focus on individual components, such as experimental setups or software tools, rather than the entire chain. Our innovative approach to automating remote experiments involves designing and implementing a comprehensive framework that streamlines the setup, configuration, execution, and monitoring of these experiments across multiple domains. Our framework's key benefits include its versatility, adaptability to diverse scenarios, and modular structure, which enables the easy integration of new features and domains. To validate our framework, we conducted experiments in three distinct fields: audiovisual testing, video streaming, and telemedicine. The results of these experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in successfully integrating these complex domains.

We examine Asser's unification of the Clarkson and Scheffler conjectures concerning the directed version of the Lovasz sandbox model. Focusing on undirected graphs, we maintain the same framework as in the directed case but modify the variable assignments and sandwich inequalities. The relationship between the Lovasz theta function and the maximum eigenvalue of a graph's adjacency matrix allows for the expansion of Asser's conjecture to the realm of undirected bipartite graphs. Moreover, we introduce the total surplus and skewness of graphs as parameters to facilitate inequality expressions involving the Lovasz theta function. The total surplus and skewness not only yield improved lower bounds to the Lovasz theta function but also provide alternatives to the eigenvalue-based maximum eigenvalue lower bound.

In scanning transmission electron microscopy, a key component is the electrostatic phase plate, used to form an electron probe of sub-angstrom diameter. Various techniques have been employed to characterize and control the phase plate's properties, yet the inherent complexities of the device pose challenges for precise specification of its performance. To address this limitation, a comprehensive model has been developed to optimize the design of electrostatic phase plates, allowing users to evaluate the influence of design choices, such as fill-factor and pixel arrangement, on the probe's size, current, and coherence. Utilizing this model, a systematic investigation was conducted into the relationship between design features and properties, revealing that a specific fill-factor configuration yields the optimal balance between small probe size and high electron current. Additionally, an investigation into pixel patterns indicated that a particular arrangement can further enhance probe size at the cost of reduced electron current. The findings from this study, along with corresponding simulations, provide valuable insights for the future development and optimization of electrostatic phase plates, thereby facilitating improvements in resolution, signal strength, and imaging rate in STEM.

We present a comprehensive framework that evaluates computational performance through fundamental principles, applying this evaluation to multiple computation methods, including quantum, adiabatic, and non-equilibrium steady-state scenarios, by translating key theoretical concepts into a unified set of criteria that can be compared across different computational mechanisms.

We show that a random walk in d dimensions visits significantly more positions compared to a random walk in d+1 dimensions in the long term, despite the difference in dimensionality affecting the distribution of visited points less significantly as it increases. Additionally, we find a relatively simple formula for calculating the average number of unique positions visited by a random walk in d dimensions, and confirm that this average increases without limit as d grows infinitely towards the right.

We explore an spherically symmetric, four-dimensional solution to the Einstein equations in the presence of a polymer modified theory of General Relativity, where the challenge of black hole or wormhole formation arises from the absence of a consistent, well-defined quantum gravity theory. Initially, the resulting equations appear intricate due to the non-trivial nature of the Lagrange constraints, but simplify to a manageable form. Several properties, including energy conditions, Cauchy surface topology, and causal structure, are examined for both black holes and wormholes. Notably, although certain features resemble each other, the properties of wormholes are found to be distinct from those of black holes. Notably, the presence of the Godel spinors leads to a theory-rich spacetime, characterized by multiple, coexisting geodesics.

The low-frequency specific heat in doped graphene, susceptible to Fermi surface instability, is investigated using a renormalization group approach that incorporates the effects of electron-electron interactions. This approach yields a general result for the specific heat, providing a comprehensive connection to the renormalization of the quasiparticle velocity and carrier density. Specifically, the specific heat is proportional to $(\frac{K_2}{\hbar v_F}(1+\frac{K_1}{K_2}e^{\frac{\pi m_e}{k_B T})})T$, where $K_1$ and $K_2$ are constants associated with electron-electron interactions, $m_e$ is the electron mass, and $v_F$ is the quasiparticle velocity. Graphene's velocity renormalization and carrier density by order of interaction power are calculated as $Z_2 = 1 + \frac{K_1}{K_2} + \cdots$ and $n = const + \frac{K_2}{Z_2} + \cdots$, with the leading term interactions given by $const = \frac{3}{8}\frac{m_e v_F^2}{\hbar^2} (K_1 + \cdots)$. The approach also determines the quasiparticle velocity renormalization to the fourth order of interaction, and obtains the density of states at the Fermi level as a function

Recent advances in neural text synthesis have led to significant improvements in the quality and variety of generated text. However, the field of neural speech synthesis still struggles with limitations in the quality and diversity of synthesized speech, particularly regarding its ability to convey emotional and social cues. To address these limitations, we propose MaskedSpeech, a generative model designed to synthesize more naturally expressive speech by learning from a diverse range of social and emotional cues within vast linguistic corpora. By incorporating a world model that incorporates social and emotional context, as well as a phoneme-level mask that preserves essential linguistic structures, MaskedSpeech is able to produce high-quality, expressive speech synthesis that surpasses existing benchmarks in naturalness and variability.

Variable selection is a fundamental process in modeling. Although sparse regression models can achieve this selection, they often sacrifice posterior uncertainty for parsimony. Sparsity-inducing penalties, which generate multiple local optima, disrupt the posterior distribution, making it difficult to capture uncertainties in coefficients. We introduce a novel sparsity-aware Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling method that explores the posterior distribution under l1 and l0 penalties while retaining the original posterior uncertainties from the unconstrained Gaussian Bayesian model. This approach incorporates a relaxed l0 penalty variable selection step, ensuring sparse models are generated. We combine this method with a robust, efficient sampling technique within a hierarchical Bayesian framework for Bayesian variable selection. This method is applied to simulated data and the US Pima dataset, demonstrating the maintenance of original uncertainties and accurate variable selection.

Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to adversarial attacks, which can manipulate them into making incorrect predictions. These attacks, typically launched locally against a trained model, differ from a sophisticated Man-in-the-Middle attack that intercepts communication between a DNN and its user. We propose a new MIM attack strategy designed for DNNs with robust local defenses, involving subtle modifications to transmitted data that aim to deceive the model without affecting its operation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach against various models, datasets, and attack methods, including a significant success rate of 87.63% on the CleverHans dataset. Furthermore, we developed an open-source implementation of our attack, which can be accessed at https://github.com/farhadi-mehdi/MIM-Attack.

Climate change conspiracy theories have been circulating for decades, with a significant proportion stemming from a single social group. Despite the potential for harm, research on climate change conspiracy theories remains limited, with existing studies often relying on small, online surveys to gather information. This study utilised a qualitative, thematic approach to analyse a significant corpus of 28,034 comments from online forums, comprising 2,884 unique individuals. Our analysis reveals the prevalent presence of conspiracy theory-related content is largely driven by a single social group, with a more significant proportion of these ideas being shared compared to other social groups. Additionally, our results indicate that understanding social group dynamics and divisions within online discussions is crucial in mitigating the spread of conspiracy theories.

Using a combined approach, combining data from LHC searches and dark matter observations, a study examines dual resolutions to the $h\to ZZ^\ast$ decay based on theoretical models involving extra fermions. In these models, a second $SU(2)_L$ doublet of fermions is introduced, where one of its components, $D$, decays into a dark matter particle and a neutrino. Additionally, a dark photon is introduced that can mediate the dark matter neutrino interaction. Analyzing final states containing four leptons, two jets, and two jets with two leptons, the research looks for signs of extra fermions in theories beyond the standard model. With standard model predictions as a baseline, statistical analysis reveals no evidence of deviation, resulting in limits on the coupling between the two doublets, yielding a coupling strength lower than $0.30$ for a certain mass range. Furthermore, the research explores various scenarios of dark matter composition, including cases where the dark matter consists of a mixture of bosons and fermions, as well as a solitary component, imposing stricter limits on the coupling strength in these scenarios.

This passage discusses the extension of dualities to exangulated categories. It is demonstrated that for an additive abelian category with a dualising object in the derived category, the corresponding exangulated completion exhibits Serre duality if and only if the category satisfies a specific condition. Furthermore, it is proven that for such a category with Serre duality, the exangulated structure can be equivalently defined using Serre duality instead of the dualising object, and that this exangulated category will have a strong dualisation pair. Additionally, it is shown that for a weak Calabi-Yau category, the derived derived Serre duality holds, allowing for the extension of weak Calabi-Yau structures to exangulated completions and strong Calabi-Yau structures to exangulated categories with Serre duality.

This study provides earnings data for fields of study in Norway, utilizing the labor market relevant data collected from tax authorities. In contrast to other national statistics offices, this data is accessible without restrictions. The research offers earnings figures for specific fields of study in Norway. It also compares these figures to those in Denmark and Sweden. One notable observation is that the earnings payoffs to post-secondary education in Norway appear to be lower than in Denmark and Sweden. One potential explanation is that the data highlights a lack of alignment between the skills acquired through vocational training and the skills demanded by the labor market.

A new generation of experiments is needed to fully explore the potential of future subatomic research beyond what's currently possible with the LHC. A high-energy particle collider that produces $J/\psi$ particles more frequently than currently possible with the LHCb experiment could potentially discover new information about antimatter, short-lived subatomic particles, and the forces governing these particles. To achieve this, a new detector is required with improved sensitivity to detect $J/\psi$ particles more efficiently. Research proposals include utilizing existing infrastructure at CERN to build a super $J/\psi$ factory, exploring new technologies to construct a high-energy particle collider, and developing innovative detector concepts to maximize discovery potential in a high-energy environment.

We conducted three-dimensional hydrodwarf simulations to study the accretion
process in a hierarchical binary-protostar system. The smaller binary within
the system was represented by a baricenter model, while interactions with the
surrounding gas were the main focus of the study. Unlike a single star of equal
mass, the binary's accretion rate was significantly lower and constant over
time, causing the protostar to form more slowly. Furthermore, angular
momentum conservation led to an outer disk developing from the gas that the
binary couldn't catch, which eventually fragmented into multiple sub-systems
that could potentially form additional stars.

We studied how matter inequalities in the early universe impact its overall shape using both mathematical theories and computer simulations. Our simulations of the universe's growth showed that matter inequalities influence its overall shape, leading to changes from an initially uniform to a more complex configuration. We analyzed these changes using two approaches: calculating the scalar factor dynamics using mathematical equations and running computer simulations of the universe's growth. Our findings suggest that matter inequalities contribute to the universe's complex shape, with potential implications for understanding its development in the early stages.

We investigate the segmentation of noisy images using the piecewise constant Mumford-Shah model under the assumption of additive Gaussian noise. To improve this model's efficiency, we modify it into the DWPCUMS model, which introduces an adjustable weight in the Mumford-Shah term's total variation seminorm. This modification enables the use of faster and more accurate numerical methods for minimizing the weighted term, while also allowing for the recovery of better segmentation results. We develop an algorithm using Bregman iterations and prove its convergence under certain conditions. Furthermore, we conduct experiments to validate the effectiveness of the DWPCUMS model and assess its sensitivity to the noise-correlated parameter.

The maximum velocity of light particles, which have mass less than the protons', can be linked to the expansion rate of the universe by a specific relationship. This relationship suggests that the velocity of these particles is directly proportional to the rate of expansion and is independent of the speed of light.
