To address these challenges, we introduce a novel co-imitation learning framework called Maximum Likelihood Co-Imitation Learning (MLCIL). By maximizing the likelihood of mimicking multiple policies, MLCIL integrates information from both expert demonstrations and reward signals. We evaluate the efficacy of our method on two complex robotic tasks: inserting a cup into a coffee filter and folding a T-shirt. The results indicate that MLCIL yields higher performance compared to traditional methods, with MLCIL achieving speeds 2.5 times faster while maintaining similar success rates as demonstration-based imitation learning. Moreover, MLCIL outperforms reward-shaping approaches by 20%, showcasing its ability to extract relevant information from sparse and imperfect reward signals.

This research examines a discrete-time binary sequential decoding problem employing the Viterbi algorithm, with a twist: instead of traditional fixed-rate cutoff methods, we utilize a rate that changes adaptively in response to the decoder's confidence level. Specifically, we investigate the probability of the decoder making mistakes when the cutoff rate is linked to the decoder's posterior probability. We develop asymptotic formulas for this error probability in situations where the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is either extremely high or extremely low. When the SNR is very high, the error probability is found to be equivalent to the probability of the decoder terminating prematurely, with an associated asymptotic rate function that resembles a modified version of the classical rate function for binary hypothesis testing. In contrast, when the SNR is very low, the error probability is found to converge to a value less than 1, with an asymptotic rate function that differs from its high-SNR counterpart. Notably, we demonstrate that choosing the polarized cutoff rate as a bias value yields a significantly reduced error probability compared to other cutoff methods.

Recent research has made significant progress in tracking hands and objects within desktop environments using a single RGB camera. Nonetheless, existing methods often struggle with occlusion challenges when hands cover objects or vice versa. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel hand-tracking approach that incorporates context-based object detection to mitigate the effects of occlusions. By leveraging contextual information, our method enables the detection of objects even when partially occluded or interacted with by hands. To improve accuracy in occluded regions, we employ a context-based object detection technique that uses pre-trained object detectors trained on desktop datasets. Context-based object detection involves using an object's mask to guide the detection process on the occluded area, thus improving interaction tracking performance. A similar technique is applied to hand tracking, using an approach based on part affordances to guide the detection process on hand parts. A context-based object detection module is incorporated into the interaction tracking pipeline to provide high-accuracy interactions even in the presence of occlusions. Experimental results demonstrate the performance of our method on interactive tracking, showing improved results on interactions involving vision-based hand-object recognition.

This paper builds upon the work started in [arXiv:2103.05173], where we classified finite groups that are reduced over a given finite field but not over its prime power. In this continuation, we classify such groups for specific cases where the base field is not a prime power, expanding our previous findings in [arXiv:2103.05173].

Our proposed method addresses a fundamental challenge in
robotic grasping, namely end-effector pose estimation. A camera attached
to the robot's base captures the environment in 3D and feeds the image
into a neural network, which outputs a pose for the end effector. Notably,
our approach can operate in environments with little to no structure for
pose estimation, and has been rigorously tested in both simulated and
real-world scenarios. Furthermore, the incorporation of a depth camera
significantly enhances the robustness of the pose estimation. Data show
that a learned point-cloud based method outperforms conventional approaches
dependent on environment features, and that the incorporation of a depth
camera surpasses performance in the scenario lacking the depth sensor.

Identifying anomalous behavior within experimental data is crucial in identifying
unanticipated phenomena. We've developed an approach, based on the use of
outlier analysis, to detect unusual patterns in electron beam data at Fermilab's
CEBAF accelerator. By focusing on individual beam positions within each
revolution, as opposed to using the standard time-domain approach, we're able to
reveal anomalies more effectively. As a result, our method has proven to be
highly valuable in detecting irregularities during recent low-current operation
runs, including both intentional and unintentional disruptions to the beam
trajectory.

The presence of dark matter in a neutron star can be detected through changes
in its surface temperature due to the release of bound dark matter particles.
Mathematically, this phenomenon is represented by the partial differential equation
$\partial_t\rho=\Delta(\rho-\rho_\infty)+\rho_0\exp(\beta\phi)\rho_0/\kappa$
with the boundary conditions $\partial_n\rho=0$ on $\partial\Omega$, and is
solved using the method of Fujita decay with the estimate $(\rho_0-\rho_\infty)\sim
e^{-t/\tau_0}\sim r^{-9}$ for large spatial distances, where $\rho_0$ and $\rho_\infty$
represent the initial and limiting densities, and $\beta$ and $\kappa$ represent
the gravitational and diffusion constants, respectively.

Weak-lensing research relies heavily on precise galaxy shape measurements. The pipeline, ShapePipe, incorporates a unique combination of adaptive convolutional neural networks and traditional galaxy shape measurement techniques to achieve this goal. Comprising four distinct components, each addressing a unique shape measurement challenge, ShapePipe efficiently handles diverse galaxy populations. We present a detailed explanation of each shape measurement module within ShapePipe and evaluate its effectiveness by comparing it to individual runs of established methods, including BPZ, NGP, and GaPipe, on real-world data. Our analysis, conducted on the SDSS dataset, reveals that the four-module pipeline consistently outperforms these comparisons at all signal-to-noise ratios. The pipeline's performance gains stem from its adaptive response to various galaxy types and its ability to leverage GaPipe's results, which had previously been computed, to remove bias in shape measurement. By combining GaPipe's results with the adaptive convolutional neural networks, ShapePipe achieves the most precise shape measurements across multiple signal-to-noise ratios. The use of ShapePipe in the SDSS dataset results in a 15% reduction in shape-measurement bias relative to BPZ, a 10% reduction relative to NGP, and a 5% reduction relative to GaPipe. The implementation of ShapePipe, along with its necessary files and documentation, is now available for download at https://github.com/ShapePipe/ShapePipe.

Inspired by the Veech discrete 2-circle problem, we examined a variant of its formulation, focusing on the domain consisting of two circles with finitely pruned orbits under the action of their common group of isometries. This investigation led us to the concept of'modified surfaces,' which we utilized to establish connections between the associated geodesic flow and those from certain well-known ensembles, such as the Chaudhuri-McMullen parametrization and the Henley-McMullen circle packing. Building upon this connection, we proposed a conjecture regarding the achievable parameters for the Chaudhuri-McMullen parametrization, which we verified in numerous non-arithmetic cases.

We provide a detailed proof of a rationality criterion for complex hypersurfaces of multi-sections in projective space, connecting to K-rationality concepts previously studied by Brückler and Nucci. The criterion involves a new concept, the minimal exponent of a polynomial, leading to a simplified understanding. Additionally, we identify a necessary and sufficient condition for K-rationality in terms of this minimal exponent, which extends a previous finding by Brückler. Furthermore, we establish that two specific parameters, the degree and codimension, control the size of the K-rationality parameter, denoted as k-rationality, and express the k-rationality parameter as an extension of the K-rationality parameter of a line segment, with which it shares key properties.

To address the persistent controversy surrounding the quantum spin liquid state in the prototypical material [Cu(pz)$_2$(2-HOpy)$_2$](PF$_6$)$_2$, our team employed a highly advanced neutron scattering technique combined with a sophisticated theoretical model to re-examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling, intermolecular interactions, and quantum fluctuations in the material. Notably, we found that the spin fluctuations are severely damped in a strong magnetic field, indicating a significant impact of field-induced magnetic ordering on the spin correlations. Moreover, we developed a groundbreaking theoretical approach for simulating quantum spin liquids using advanced machine learning algorithms, thereby enabling the accurate simulation of quantum spin liquids. Our simulation results reveal a spin-liquid phase at zero field, in alignment with experimental findings, and also predict the existence of a field-induced magnetic ordering phenomenon. Furthermore, we discovered that the application of magnetic field leads to the emergence of a long-range order of a'striped cupric k2 structure', characterized by incommensurate magnetic correlations. In contrast, we found that the spin fluctuations are not significantly affected by the application of pressure, suggesting its relatively minor impact compared to magnetic field. Our integrated experimental and theoretical research sheds new light on the complex phase behavior of the material and clarifies previously unresolved issues, thereby providing a comprehensive understanding of the quantum spin liquid state in [Cu(pz)$_2$(2-HOpy)$_2$](PF$_6$)$_2$.

A new model called $a\mu$MSM is developed within the framework of the Infrasound sector, featuring a non-compact $U(1)$ symmetry to account for the axion's role in solving the strong CP problem and addressing the electroweak vacuum stabilization issue. The model includes a minimal set of scalar fields, with a quartic potential designed to generate the correct cosmological scale for perturbative coherence, and a mass ratio for the muon and electron consistent with observed values. The model predicts a model-dependent range for the axion decay constant, $10^{16}\,{\rm GeV} < f_a < 10^{20}\,{\rm GeV}$.

In this study, we examine the classical simulation of quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates, employing a key variation of the standard Markov chain dynamics used in simulation. Our proposed method builds upon a prior algorithm by Shor, which was later enhanced by Monte Carlo integration by Childs, Maslov, and Yao. Our new approach reduces the simulation time to $\Theta(4^d)$ from $\Theta(2^d)$ in the number of qubits $d$, resulting in a significant improvement for large-scale simulations. Our findings show that this algorithm efficiently estimates the output probability for a $\eta$-accurate approximation within time $O(\eta^{-2}\log^3(1\eta))$. Our results further reveal that this algorithm can be adapted for realistic simulation on classical hardware with very minimal modifications, using a technique known as "staging". Our staged algorithm requires $2.25$ stages, which contrasts with the $4.5$ stages required by a previous algorithm by Zou et al., necessitating only minor changes to their dynamic process. Our simulation results validate the efficiency and accuracy of our algorithm in both theoretical and practical scenarios.

A new framework, the Tsallis holographic dark energy (THDE) model, incorporates interacting coupling and a coupling parameter related to the holographic mass scale $\Lambda_{THDE}$, which is in contrast to the standard non-interacting dark energy models. This paper investigates the interaction between matter and dark energy in the THDE framework using the Hubble parameter data sets from CNRS, CNRST, University of Johannesburg, and University of Wisconsin Observatory databases with varying values of the parameter $q_0$. Our analysis shows that the datasets are consistent with each other, and we find evidence of interaction between matter and dark energy for $q_0$ in the range $0.5001 to 0.5034$. Additionally, we calculate the coupling parameter $\gamma$ in terms of $q_0$ as $ \gamma = (1-\omega_0)/ (1+\omega_0) * (q_0+0.5)$. Furthermore, we found that the value of $\Lambda_{THDE}$ is equal to $(1-\omega_0) * (q_0+0.5)$. Our analysis using CNRS dataset also gives the value of $\gamma$ as $0.6168  \pm 0.2207$ with $1\sigma$ uncertainty in consistency with the standard parameter $q_0$ for the first time.

In 2019, the LAMOST Time-domain Survey initiated a study of binary star systems across various Galactic populations.  This survey utilized data from both the LAMOST double star catalog and a range of binary candidates from the Open Galaxy Catalogue, resulting in a comprehensive binary catalog containing 1029 entries.  Through an analysis of orbital periods and distribution, the data revealed significant differences between binary populations in the Galactic disk and halo.  Furthermore, the findings suggest an influence of environmental factors on the binary systems, implying a possible link to the binary star formation mechanism.  This research employed advanced techniques including the Park scale period method and a binary detection reliability assessment.  By utilizing the LAMOST multi-fiber spectrograph's high signal-to-noise ratio spectral data, the study's results show great promise for future studies of binary star systems.

In recent years, trustzone-based random number generators (TRNGs) have gained 
attention due to their capabilities in producing high-quality random numbers. 
However, current designs often involve flaws such as non-cryptographic quality 
random number generation, excessive energy consumption, and limited generation 
capacity. To address these shortcomings, we develop the TuRaN generator, an 
innovative solution enhancing random number quality while decreasing energy usage 
and elevating throughput capacity. The TuRaN generator utilizes a combined 
architecture of statistical and physical analysis, incorporating an integrity 
checker and error-correction modules to produce high-quality random numbers. 
Furthermore, it implements a sliding-block approach to maximize efficiency and 
increase throughput. The generator is designed with compatibility in mind and 
can be integrated into a variety of systems, including ARM, PowerPC, and 
MIPS processors. A practical implementation of the TuRaN generator is demonstrated 
using the OMAP3530, a dual-core Texas Instruments processor, which showcases 
its ability to produce 214.5 bits of random numbers every 4.4 microseconds while 
consumming 8.6 nano-amperes of current.

The concept of a single-electron resistive switch, initially proposed in 2000, is experiencing a resurgence in interest due to advances in nanotechnology. This revival is driven by the potential for ultra-compact single-electron devices, including switches, which could significantly improve energy efficiency in electronic devices. The switch design involves a tiny gap in a material that can conduct electricity, and properties are defined by the presence of a single electron within this gap. Research has shown that carbon nanotubes are suitable materials for constructing such a gap. In experiments, carbon nanotubes have demonstrated the ability to withstand high levels of electric voltage without failing, and by combining multiple nanotubes, researchers have built robust single-electron devices capable of withstanding external interference. By utilizing special techniques to control the chemical composition of the nanotubes, researchers have developed switches with exceptional properties, including high on/off current ratios and fast switching speeds. These advanced single-electron switches offer great potential for use in extremely compact devices, including logic circuits, where their unique properties could greatly reduce power consumption.

To analyze multi-loop Feynman integrands and identify their causal properties, we develop a novel technique that transforms Feynman integrands into causal configurations through a graphical expansion. This method allows us to decode the internal structure of Feynman integrands and reveal their causal associations, which form the basis of our theorem proving strategy for loop topology verification. Utilizing this approach, we develop a framework for rapidly verifying the loop topologies of Feynman integrands, even for complex scenarios involving numerous loops and connections. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical application of this framework by successfully verifying the loop structures in planar triple-loop scattering processes, an essential precursor to thorough calculations of this scenario.

We examine certain aspects of Green functions associated with quantum walks on graphs, specifically their connection to the spectral measures derived from the Dyson-Schrieffer equations in the study of quantum mechanics. This analysis enables us to define a quantum walk's Green functions relative to any given boundary condition, thereby broadening the applicability of the term "Green functions" beyond their traditional link to stochastic processes. Furthermore, we explore relationships between Green functions, both in the discrete and continuous contexts, and establish a duality theorem that reveals a symmetry between the Green functions of a graph and its complement.

This study delves into hybrid stars composed of neutrons, protons, and quarks, 
using the two relativistic mean field models for quark phase descriptions 
and four distinct equations of state for neutron-proton matter. 
Specifically, we examine the mass-radius relations of hybrid stars 
and examine the consequences of varying the quark core radius and core 
mass fraction on this problem. 
Our analysis indicates that even a small quark core can lead to hybrid stars 
with substantially larger radii than those observed for neutron stars. 
Furthermore, we verify that the mass-radius relations of hybrid stars conform 
to the observed limits for neutron stars, thereby fulfilling the necessary 
conditions for possible hybrid star candidates. 
This research aims to provide insights into the possible impact of quark cores 
on the mass-radius relationships of compact stars.

We investigate a novel optical model incorporating both tunneling and optomechanical interactions, characterized by a non-commutative relationship between position and momentum, denoted as $[x, p] = i\hbar G_0$. Introducing a tunable tunneling parameter $\kappa$, we find that shifting it from a non-zero value to zero effectively decouples the two wells in the probe field, resonances, and phonon populations. Furthermore, increasing optomechanical coupling $\chi$ causes the probe field to bifurcate into two distinct amplitude patterns, which are stable yet reversibly switchable with tunable parameters $\kappa$. We observe similar behavior in the resonances and phonon populations, and we describe the dynamics of this system within a three-dimensional space, defining a circuit that starts at a symmetric point and evolves towards a tripartite equilibrium, separated into distinct phases by lines that connect the initial symmetric state to this tripartite point.

Within the framework of the fermionic clustered nuclear shell model, young operator basis is used to calculate the 2+ scissors modes associated with the core $^{40}$Ca. The study incorporates F5 two-body interactions from the DD-ME-Christopher potential, which distinguishes R-negative from positive scissors modes via electromagnetic transition strengths and energies. The largest eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian, transition probabilities, and R-ratios were extracted for each spin-parity pair. The 2+ states, characterized by specific $d_{x2-y2}$ angular momentum components, exhibit significant differences between positive and negative patterns, with the latter typically displaying lower energies, stronger transitions and an inverted R/2 ratio compared to their positive counterparts. The highest R-values were found in the $d_{3z}$ operator, which indicates that negative scissors modes have more contracted, toroidal shapes, whereas positive modes are longer and thinner.

We investigated the electronic properties of Ba$_{1-x}$Na$_x$V$_2$O$_4$ through thickness-driven tuning of the metal-insulator transition. Our results reveal a unique scenario where the transition can be finely tuned by both chemical doping and dimensional changes. Upon reducing thickness below a certain critical point, Ba$_{1-x}$Na$_x$V$_2$O4$ undergoes a metal-insulator transition, characterized by a rapid increase in resistance with diminishing thickness. In the thickest insulating state, the material exhibits a pseudogap at the Fermi level, whereas in the thinest metal state, this pseudogap closes, revealing well-developed three-dimensional electronic properties. In the intermediate thickness regime, we observe a hybrid metal-insulator state with a weakly developed pseudogap. These findings suggest that the electronic properties of Ba$_{1-x}$Na$_x$V$_2$O4$ are interlinked, with dimensional flexibility offering a means to adjust the intensity of the pseudogap until the material transitions into a 3D electronic state. Furthermore, we utilized high-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) to investigate the thickness-dependent evolution of the quasiparticle band structure. In the thickest insulating state, the quasiparticle weight at the Fermi level is minuscule, whereas in the thinest metal state, the weight significantly increases. In the intermediate thickness regime,

The cooling plateau in laser-cooled atomic ensembles is reached when the entropy remains constant, driven by the trade-off between entropy reduction from cooling and entropy increase from collisional heating. Our analysis shows that this constant entropy value is directly tied to the ensemble's initial distribution and the parameters of the velocity model. For more complex models of velocity distribution, considering multiple dimensional models, the behavior becomes even more reliant on the distribution's specific characteristics. However, in cases where the distribution has distinct, isolated groups with varying temperatures, the entropy increase from collisional heating outweighs the entropy reduction from cooling, leading to an ever-increasing entropy and a never-reached plateau. This outcome is reminiscent of the model describing the ensemble as a fractal, with the collisional heating causing its dimensions to expand. Our findings also imply that achieving this plateau requires either a custom-tailored velocity distribution or using a customized, complex velocity model.

Our study utilizes a complex network approach to examine the structure of the Cryptocurrency Trading Network (CTN) from 2020 to 2021.  Analyzing weekly transaction data, we constructed a time-evolving network to understand the development of CTN.  Our results reveal that the trading network exhibits small-world and fractal characteristics, in addition to displaying significant growth in both the number of nodes and edges.  However, this increase was largely contained within the core of the network, as its periphery remained relatively constant.  Our findings also indicate that the core of the network operates on a logarithmic timescale.  Similar to other financial systems, CTN is prone to cascading failures and polarization due to its interconnected components.  As the network continued to expand, its complexity reached a peak in the first half of 2021, after which it began to stabilize.  In contrast, the volatility of Cryptocurrency prices exhibited irregular behavior.  Our research suggests that the core of CTN can be utilized as a potential early warning system for predicting price fluctuations and instability, given its ability to anticipate significant events.

Proton transfer between a water molecule and two sulphuric acid molecules, positioned in an octahedral configuration, is investigated using quantum mechanics and electrostatic potential surfaces derived from quantum chemistry methods. Accounting for the vibrational motion of nuclei, as predicted by path integral mechanics, reveals that this motion significantly impacts proton transfer pathways. Focusing on the lowest lying proton transfer state, which exhibits a semi-classical behavior, reveals that the proton's path is akin to a stochastic trajectory, influenced by the strong electrostatic potential. Moreover, the probability distribution of the proton's position along the pathway to transfer is evenly distributed between the two water and acid molecules, except during the actual transfer process. Furthermore, at 300 Kelvin nuclear zero-point motion accelerates the proton transfer by a factor of three, compared to a model that assumes static nuclei.

This research builds on the findings of G. Acs' paper [arXiv:1803.01370], providing additional insights and broader applications. We establish that the space of group-equivariant, non-expansive operators is isometrically embedded within a compact space when the group action is transitive or unimodular. Furthermore, we expand the concepts of equivariance and non-expansiveness to arbitrary metrics, and explore connections with quantum conditional mean independence.

We model a small molecule moving within a cellular transport system, assuming it moves independently from the surrounding medium, which may have a temperature gradient. This situation prompts the use of a two-state model, where the molecule can be in two distinct states: mobile or stationary, to analyze its motion under the influence of thermal parameters. We discovered that the normal Einstein relation does not hold in this scenario due to the impact of differences in molecular weights and a parameter representing the resistance to movement. However, the relation can be modified to account for the molecule's mass and a new parameter. Additionally, we derived an expression for how this parameter affects the diffusion coefficient. We also found a way to measure this parameter by analyzing the distribution of time intervals between the molecule's transitions from the stationary state. As a practical application, our model could potentially aid in understanding how certain molecules work as thermometers in cells, potentially improving methods for measuring temperature changes within living organisms.

In deep learning research, researchers often test various training heuristics but
the influence of these tests is usually limited to improving models already
designed. Conversely, our research investigates how different training methods
affect the development of model complexity. By implementing a regularisation
technique on weight norms, we examine the effect on model capacity and,
subsequently, test its implications on generalisation performance. By doing so,
we identify a previously unseen pattern in model performance, which suggests
that models performing well on training data may actually exhibit characteristics
unfavorable to future generalisation.

We introduce an alternative method of fitting which, in the context of unbinned data, provides a more precise determination of kinematic parameters in particle decay processes that are governed by a linear motion. This method builds upon the use of likelihood functions and takes advantage of the continuous nature of momentum and energy data. In contrast to traditional methods that divide data into bins, our approach offers improved resolution and reduced uncertainties. The implementation of our method is illustrated through simulations of a muon decay at rest, and simulations of Z-bosons decaying into electrons and muons, utilising Monte Carlo samples generated by MadGraph5.

To effectively evaluate models for automated essay grading, a comprehensive dataset of prompts and answers was created, based on a diverse collection of 1,037 exam questions from the COCO-Challenge. The dataset is called AutoGrade Challenge and comprises four parts: an initial evaluation subset and three larger datasets used for training, cross-validation, and testing. A range of machine learning models was developed to tackle the complex task at hand. The strategies employed for enhancing model performance involved custom data augmentation methods, the use of Word2Vec for special token distribution, and a novel attention mechanism that prioritizes critical information. The development process involved advanced cross-validation techniques and an innovative evaluation metric system. The resulting models demonstrated exceptional potential in automated essay grading, achieving scores of 64.96% for key phrase matching and 34.30% for sentence-level evaluation, with a cross-correlation coefficient of 0.671 for multi-task learning between score prediction and key phrase matching.

We focus on maintaining confidentiality when collecting sensitive data, specifically considering models that rely on marginal independence and two common estimation techniques: maximum likelihood and Bayesian methods. The utility theory basis of these models is discussed along with the constraints of dominant utility and the absence of utility dominance. We establish that utility-decency is a necessary condition both for maintaining confidentiality with maximum likelihood estimation and for generating posterior distributions that respect confidentiality. Furthermore, this condition can be fulfilled in the context of utility-constrained optimization, and we provide an approach to tackle this constraint. In contrast, Bayesian methods face a challenge as they typically struggle with the issue of utility-decency due to the inherent nature of their prior distributions. An alternative approach, belief distribution learning, is proposed and shown to be more effective in generating confidential distributions compared to traditional Bayesian methods.

This research develops a society model in which individuals' socioeconomic circumstances are determined by their genetic makeup and the opportunities available to them, and applies a mathematical approach known as stochastic dynamics to examine the likelihood of advantageous genetic mutations rising over time, ultimately resulting in improved overall fitness. Our findings demonstrate that the director of societal opportunity policy can undertake actions in the present that yield beneficial outcomes for future generations, and we present a graphical tool to help directors make informed decisions by identifying the optimal opportunity distribution for their progeny's benefit.

We develop a straightforward, physically motivated approach to understanding the phase factor that results from coordinating the permutation of multiple particles. In this context, particles with half-integral spin are represented by a specific geometric interpretation, whereas particles with integral spin are treated as a combination of half-integral spin particles. Consequently, we derive a general formula for the sign factor associated with the permutation of $N$ particles with arbitrary spin, and discuss several key mathematical properties related to this permutation. Specifically, we establish the identity that the number of permutations with a particular sign factor equals the dimension of the corresponding irreducible representation in the group of spin symmetries corresponding to that representation. We then utilize this property to calculate a specific sum over all possible sign factors for permutations of $N$ particles with arbitrary spin, and show that this sum equals the total number of permutations of $N$ particles, which is equal to $N!$. The results obtained are consistent with the principles of quantum mechanics, and serve as a fundamental foundation for further investigation into the signs associated with the permutation of $N$ particles with arbitrary spin under the constraints of wavefunction antisymmetry.

Recently introduced RingCT (Ring Central Transparency) revolutionized cryptocurrencies by allowing for ring signatures in coins, but its limitations restrict a single transaction to about ten signatures, making it inefficient for large-scale payments. To overcome this constraint, Delegated RingCT was conceived but it has several drawbacks, primarily due to its reliance on an centralized authority, which poses significant security risks in decentralized systems. To address these issues, this paper presents a new Delegated RingCT protocol that eliminates the need for a centralized authority, replacing it with a consensus mechanism that allows a group of users to make collective decisions on payment distribution. We have developed a simulation program to test the performance of Delegated RingCT and the results indicate its compatibility with existing Bitcoin wallets, while significantly enhancing transaction speed and scalability.

Our findings relate to solving linear systems of equations, specifically in the context of polynomial-time solutions. An important concept in this area is the idea of an approximate solver for a linear system, which can generate solutions with certain bounded errors relative to optimal solutions. Researchers have discovered that for certain types of linear systems, approximate solvers can be linked to circuit complexity. This idea has implications for other problems, such as finding independent sets in graph structures. To further understand this concept, researchers have created a framework that allows them to express relationships between approximate solvers and circuit complexity. This framework involves proving a key theorem that connects solving linear systems to circuit complexity, by reducing complex problems with known solutions to simpler ones. To demonstrate the utility of this concept, researchers have provided examples, such as proving that finding independent sets in certain types of graph structures is a difficult problem, especially in terms of parametrized complexity. This framework also allows for the expression of relationships between approximate solvers, such as reducing the complexity of one solver to that of another. This concept has implications for other problems, such as finding independent sets and verifying graph matching configurations.

A study examining individual production of W boson pairs in final states with two leptons and two jets at the LHC, utilizing data collected with the CMS detector at 13 TeV, is presented. This study utilizes 35.9 fb^-1 of data, enabling the measurement of WZ production with an observed significance of 3.4 standard deviations, and WW production with an observed significance of 4.0 standard deviations. Cross sections for these processes are calculated at a next-to-leading order QCD scale of 175 GeV, with the measured total cross sections being 21.2 +/- 5.2 fb and 6.4 +/- 2.1 fb for WZ and WW production, respectively. These measurements are in agreement with theoretical predictions from the Next-to- Leading Order Standard Model.

This paper presents our findings on the initial results from the CoNLL 2021 shared task, specifically task 1, which focused on comprehensive Universal Dependencies (UD) annotations for the Hebrew language. The development of a new UD treebank for Modern Hebrew enabled researchers to achieve state-of-the-art benchmarks in NLP for the language. The shared task featured three essential tasks: part-of-speech and chunk tagging, dependency parsing, and sentence splitting. We submitted two models for evaluation, incorporating the new UD treebank and leveraging the Rapid Automatic Speech Recognition system dataset. Our models displayed exceptional performance, achieving outstanding results in all three tasks, with particularly remarkable gains in dependency parsing and sentence splitting. We also introduced a novel approach using RBergamot to generate RST trees, which significantly improved performance in sentence splitting. Our techniques and dataset innovations are expected to enhance the development of UD treebanks in related Semitic languages.

For many years, researchers have been trying to find a way to use linear operators to reduce the dimensionality of unit ball spaces in various norms while achieving the highest possible level of accuracy. This problem has been resolved for the Euclidean norm, but it remains an open question for other norms. In this paper, we show that no linear transformation can reduce the dimensionality of the l1 unit ball by more than a linear factor, and if the dimensionality reduction is not strictly linear, then the error in its Euclidean form increases exponentially with the dimension. This result is surprising because the standard epsilon-isometric dimension reduction algorithm works so well for the l2 norm. To understand this phenomenon, we analyzed the error in l1 norm and found that it behaves differently from the error in the l2 norm, resulting in an exponential gap between the best possible dimensionality reduction algorithms for these two norms.

To address the issue of a material's history-dependent plasticity in solid mechanics, 
we necessitate a method that enables continuous learning and updates based on new 
experimental data without necessitating the retraining of the model with all previously 
collected data. This challenge mirrors that in the field of Continual Learning in deep 
machine learning, specifically in the scenario of incremental learning. By adapting 
existing Continual Learning methods to neural networks, we develop a new approach that 
enables the modeling of a material's plasticity behavior over time. This approach is 
extensive in scope, encompassing all loss within-the-task, learning regularization, 
and example methods that reduce dependence on prior data. We demonstrate the efficacy 
of this method by continuously updating a model of single-crystal 3D printing, 
initially trained on compressive loading data, to accurately model subsequent in-plane 
tensile and shear loading conditions.

Researchers examined the performance of various factor graphs utilizing Gallager's distribution, both with and without message passing decoding, and derived explicit criteria for successful operation under a given message passing decoding threshold and erasure probability. By utilizing empirical techniques and numerical simulations, it was discovered that factor graphs originating from randomly constructed LDPC, SPC, and multicoder models, frequently fail to meet the required conditions over large scales due to excessive degree-degree correlations. Consequently, this leads to a substantial reduction in the maximum permissible erasure probability for these factor graphs. Furthermore, quasi-definite programming was employed to optimize the factor graph parameters, yielding improved performance in certain scenarios. The study also observed that dense connectivities tend to minimize degree-degree correlations but may not necessarily yield the best performance. The investigators also observed that, under a given message passing decoding threshold, increasing the average degree results in reduced density of error events but may not guarantee better performance. Ultimately, it was found that dense and highly connected factor graphs frequently fail to satisfy the required conditions for successful operation over large scales due to excessive degree-degree correlations.

This introduction centers on a proposed Safety Control approach, referred to as SL-MPSF, designed to maintain system safety in the presence of bounded disturbances using minimum control effort. Building on past research involving predictive control methods, we develop an optimized strategy based on Model Predictive Control (MPC) for linear systems with constraints, incorporating safety considerations through modification of the cost function. Our approach ensures system safety by including a bounded safety area within the predictive horizon, thereby reducing the required control effort to implement safety protocols. Subsequent mathematical analysis confirms that our SL-MPC approach is viable, meaning it rarely needs to implement safety measures, and more importantly, we prove that SL-MPC is stable and reaches equilibrium quickly. To improve efficiency, we propose an iterative SL-MPC algorithm, which converges to a safety-informed equilibrium in a limited number of steps, and we further this approach by developing a slant-based iterative algorithm, which reaches a safety-informed equilibrium even faster, and sometimes surpasses traditional MPC performance by leveraging slacks.

In a general, comprehensive way, we have analyzed the security of the vacuum+weak decoy state quantum key distribution (QKD) method. Our study reveals that an unnoticeable eavesdropper can effectively exploit this system by means of a concentrated attack. We have proposed a new, improved light-matter interaction model that simulates the behavior of a real-world QKD system. Our research suggests that the generation of a weak decoy state should be carried out using a source that has its own optimal parameter settings, rather than being produced by the same source as the signal state. We have also investigated the relevant factors that influence the proposed improvement. Our results indicate that a tight bounding value can be achieved when the weak decoy state and signal state are produced by different sources. Specifically, we found that a reduced bound can be attained when the gain of the weak decoy state is much lower than that of the signal state. Our study suggests that the proposed method could enhance the security and efficiency of the vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system.

Recent advancements in few-shot in-context learning have highlighted the importance of developing language models with strong pre-training. However, the connection between a language model's pre-training evaluation metric, such as perplexity, and its performance in few-shot tasks is not well understood. To investigate this relationship, we evaluated the performance of a range of language models, including GPT-2 and T5, on a variety of intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation metrics while varying the context size in pre-training. Interestingly, our findings suggest that low perplexity does not consistently guarantee high performance in few-shot in-context learning tasks. Instead, these two criteria seem to require distinct pre-training setups and architectures. The study offers insights into the design of pre-training protocols for multi-task models.

Even with the rapid formation of the cosmic web at early epochs, the growth of cool cores in galaxy clusters remains an enigma. The traditional assumption in hydrodynamical simulations that heat diffuses isotropically has not yielded satisfactory explanations. A novel approach for non-isotropic heat conduction in clusters has been developed and incorporated into simulations of galaxy cluster formation. Results demonstrate that anisotropic thermal conduction accelerates the growth of cold cores. The inductive method used to solve the heat equation allows for various heat conduction functions to be utilized, and future modifications to include magnetic effects are feasible. Clusters formed with the new anisotropic conduction mechanism exhibit enhanced cooling rates and more pronounced core profiles than those in simulations utilizing isotropic conduction. Furthermore, the inclusion of magnetic fields in a force-free state has been found to suppress convection and influence conduction results, particularly at high magnetic field strengths. The anisotropic conduction mechanism may provide a viable solution to the long-standing challenges of modeling galaxy cluster growth.

Observations indicating CP violation in beauty baryons and charm systems have emerged, which deviates from predicted standards model outcomes. If these findings hold, they would be among the most consequential discoveries in particle physics history. We explore several theoretical models which could potentially explain these anomalies, highlighting connections to other phenomena such as dark matter formation and flavorful extensions of the electroweak sector.

We've derived new high-energy amplitudes for string scattering through the use of $\mathfrak{w}$-cohomology in both the context of the RNS worldsheet model and the superstring case. Interestingly, these results align with a 2021 proposal by Motl that string theory exhibits a simple, symmetric structure at extremely high energy levels. Notably, the newly calculated amplitudes display a pattern of decreasing complexity as energy increases, ultimately giving rise to a sequence of proportional relationships at incredibly high energy levels. Conjecturing that these properties extend indefinitely to all energy levels, we might interpret the $\mathfrak{w}$-cohomology as a unified framework for describing both the intricate, underlying physics of string theory and its more accessible, simpler aspects at the theoretical limit.

This research explores how artificial intelligence can enhance the efficiency of
computing operations in remote locations by optimizing resource usage. A deep
reinforcement learning model is developed to reduce energy expenditure at data
centres by controlling the distribution of computational tasks and machine power
within each facility. A multi-agent reinforcement learning system is designed to
coordinate data centre operations across multiple locations, promoting shared
solutions and increased cooperation. Through simulations, we demonstrate that these
strategies produce significant gains, with cooperation yielding up to a 10% improvement
in energy savings compared to centralized control.

This study proposes a novel neural model for speech that blends both transient and steady-state characteristics, mimicking how speech naturally progresses. By integrating a hierarchical encoder-decoder structure with a dynamic control system, the model produces speech that dynamically shifts between distinct phonetic states. To optimize the model, it was trained over a vast corpus combining both speech and non-speech sounds, effectively replicating the complex interplay between speech and its acoustic environment. The model was further refined through an iterative learning process guided by human feedback, resulting in a substantial improvement in its speech synthesis capabilities.

This study presents an efficient motion planning system for multi-limbed robots, developing a novel multi-stage optimization approach that incorporates optimal coordinated movements of individual limbs and swaths. The proposed methodology consists of three stages: generating a basic motion plan, refining the placement ofswaths, and precisely positioning limbs. A weighted graph is used to represent possible states and actions during each stage, which are solved using a greedy algorithm. The system's effectiveness is tested using a simulator of a quadroped robot performing a dance routine.

In quantum resource theories, discovering distillation methods for utilizing and sharing valuable states is a primary goal. Our research focuses on efficiently converting highly pure states of quantum nature into fewer but more valuable copies within the framework of qutrit systems. By applying the resource transformation framework, we develop specific tradeoff relationships between error probabilities and distillation ratios for optimally transforming certain pure state families. Our analysis also reveals that a specific tradeoff relationship is universally applicable to all pure state families, allowing for a comprehensive characterization of distillable resources in these contexts. Furthermore, our mathematical approach involves a convex geometric interpretation of tradeoff relationships using operational methods.

To investigate how a cup of coffee responds when rotated in a horizontal plane, we conducted two experiments that involved replacing the traditional handle-based method of rotation. In the first experiment, we replaced the handle with a rigid beam that allowed us to isolate the effect of the pivot point's position. By rotating the cup around different points, we observed that its behavior changes significantly, characterized by changes in both the direction and magnitude of the forces acting on it. In the second experiment, we involved three participants who acted as bartenders, navigating a cup filled with coffee using various techniques. Our results showed that the cup's motion followed a predictable pattern, consisting of a linear motion phase followed by a rotation phase, throughout which the forces acting on it remained consistent and positive. Notably, our findings challenge the widely held belief that the forces acting on a cup during rotation are unpredictable and varied greatly between participants.

In this work, a decentralized learning approach using drift-reduction (DR) is combined with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) results in the DR-DSGD algorithm. This algorithm successfully eliminates the drift issue in federated averaging (FA), allowing it to converge at a rate comparable to centralized SGD. With a convergence rate of $O(1/\sqrt{T})$, DR-DSGD meets the same accuracy standards as centralized SGD, despite facing drift-related challenges, and achieves the same level of accuracy in $T$ iterations, and does so across various network topologies and numbers of participating devices.

The production of specific particles in nucleus-nucleus collisions is examined in the context of the AMPT and UrQMD models. Analysis of entropy generation in the initial stages of the collision reveals that information theory's principle of maximum entropy applies, yielding accurate predictions for the relative abundances of particles in nucleus-nucleus and proton-proton collisions, including antiprotons. However, AMPT fails to accurately predict strange particle formation in cold nuclear matter. UrQMD, a hydrodynamically-motivated model, offers a potential solution by incorporating an equation of state parameter that aligns with recent cosmic microwave background measurements, suggesting the possibility of equilibration in high-energy nucleus-nucleus collisions via viscous heat conduction.

Within the framework of the core collapse protostar formation model, we've developed a new computational method to simulate protostar formation and early mass accretion within collapsing cores. This method accounts for the impact of magnetic forces and efficient kinetic energy release from the collision of falling bodies within the core. We identified two primary pathways that could result in the ejection of a large amount of mass from the protostar in the early stages. These pathways involve either extremely high fall-in energies releasing a substantial amount of energy near the protostar or magnetic forces that are sufficiently strong to support the protostar against incoming fall-in material. In the first scenario, we observed mass ejection comparable to that of the early protostar formation scenario, with the mass loss occurring on very short timescales. In the second scenario, we found that the mass loss occurred over a longer period and took the form of outflows with high-velocity material that could potentially explain the observed velocity patterns in the formation of the [CII] hole. System destabilizers, whether human or machine, can impair system reliability.
However, current safety control schemes focus on preventive measures, omitting
consideration for measures to mitigate hazards as they unfold.
This paper proposes a concept for an adaptive safety system that incorporates
compensatory measures for system destabilizers. It defines items that counteract
the impact of destabilizing effects and provides mathematical expressions for them.
Further, a network structure is developed to share and integrate the safety
experiences of various systems, enabling the adaptation of compensatory measures
for human destabilizers in advanced life support systems.

This research identifies and classifies the resonances triggered by Solar Radiation Pressure that affect the movement of an object in a circular orbit around the Sun-Object-Earth triangle. The study utilizes a simplified model, ignoring the object's mass and any effects of its elliptical shape, to develop equations that describe its trajectory under the influence of Solar Radiation Pressure. By applying conservation of angular momentum and analyzing the resonances in terms of orbital elements such as eccentricity, inclination, and longitude of the ascending node, the study derives expressions for resonance periods and eccentricities, which match previously proposed formulas for specific resonances. Additionally, the study provides formulas for additional resonances and their corresponding periods, identifying two unique cases where changes in inclination and eccentricity occur differently. Furthermore, the study finds that the eigenvalues associated with these resonances are complex, indicating damped oscillations. By classifying resonances based on their characteristics, the study develops a framework for identifying and detecting Solar Radiation Pressure resonances in an object's orbital path.

In modeling the electronic structure of solids using the tight-binding model, the peierls substitution in the Hamiltonian accurately describes the band structure, yet suffers from an incomplete treatment of electromagnetic responses.  This limitation is more pronounced in the velocity gauge than the scalar potential gauge.  An improved method is presented that fine-tunes the electromagnetic vector potential to accurately describe not only the band structure but also the dielectric response of the system.  This approach is based on a rigorous derivation of the Thomas-Nordheim equation governing electron field emission, which it modifies to develop a corrected electromagnetic vector potential applicable to tight-binding models.  When applied to tight-binding models, the proposed vector potential yields results that agree with first-principles calculations, including the accurate description of dielectric properties across various scales, from individual nanostructures to extended nanowires and solid-state materials.

We introduce a graph-theoretic framework for robust pose and shape estimation,
focusing on increasing the robustness of our model against outlier data.
We model the pose and shape challenge as a problem where we select a few
linear subspaces from a set of candidate subspaces containing point correspondences
between images of an object and its projections onto a grid.
We represent the subspaces as nodes in a graph, with an edge added between two
nodes if the corresponding linear subspaces contain a significant proportion of
the points in question - a condition that can be satisfied through a designated
threshold.
We aim to find a subset of minimum weight (corresponding to large inter-node
distance) where the corresponding subspaces contain a majority of the points in
question and share a significant amount of information about the object's shape
and pose.
We present an algorithm to determine the minimum weight subgraph of near-linear
complexity, where our model's parameters determine the efficiency.
We showcase our framework's effectiveness in various simulations, where it
outperforms alternatives by boosting robustness and shape estimation accuracy
while reducing computational costs.

We derive closed-form formulas for the confidence intervals of the parameters $a$, $b$, and $
u$ in the Cauchy distribution using the maximum likelihood estimation method, which leads to defining these intervals as geometric shapes in the complex plane. Specifically, the confidence region for the parameters $(a, b)$ forms a circle with radius $R$, where $R = \sqrt{(-1 + 
u) b^2 + 
u a^2}$, and the 95% confidence interval is given by $|a - b^2| > 3.182 \sqrt{1 + a^2}$, and similarly, the relationship between the radius $R$ and the parameters $a$ and $
u$ is given as $R^2 = ab(-1 + 
u)$. Furthermore, we propose an alternative method to estimate the parameters $(a, b)$ using the confidence region's geometric properties, and demonstrate the method's effectiveness through simulations in R programming language. Additionally, we outline a strategy for extending this approach to other families of skew-distributions.

In clinical trials, borrowing information between subgroups can significantly impact power, yet traditionally subgroups are treated independently.  When subgroups share a commensurate relationship, shared information can be utilized through a pooling approach.  The minimal number of observations needed for a specified level of confidence and power is significantly reduced when grouping is incorporated.  Through the application of mixed models, the estimated variance components are shared among the subgroups, creating an interdependence that increases efficiency.  The approach is straightforward to implement and results in a universal formula that can be computed quickly, even with large datasets.  The methodology is universally applicable to any type of data and can be extended to higher-dimensional grouping scenarios.  A numerical example demonstrates the benefits of this approach, showing that sample sizes can be substantially reduced when appropriate grouping is identified.

Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly impacted the field of motion control due to their ability to effectively deal with nonlinear systems, unseen data, and adaptive capabilities. However, the application of deep learning in motion control often disregards the fact that state estimation and control are highly position-dependent. Consequently, motion control systems usually require additional mechanisms, such as explicit modeling of the position, to function properly. This paper investigates the effect of position dependence on deep motion control and tracking. We develop a novel framework, consisting of a position aware neural network, to demonstrate its efficacy in motion control and tracking in multiple scenarios, including real-world applications in robotics and electromagnetics. The proposed method demonstrates adaptive capabilities and improves performance significantly when compared to conventional methods that do not consider the position dependence.

Our research focuses on transferring the features learned from a point cloud registration task to an object classification task, leveraging self-supervised learning techniques. Specifically, we utilize the geometric transformations applied during point cloud registration to create a set of augmented point clouds, which can be employed to train a classification model. By doing so, we capitalize on the pre-trained network's ability to effectively handle geometric transformations, thus streamlining the training process and improving outcomes for the object classification task. Moreover, our method yields results on real-world datasets without requiring any ground truth information, making it suitable for applications where labeled data is scarce or expensive to obtain.

This study explores the concept of $R_\infty$-nilpotency in groups, where a group $G$ with respect to a subset $R$ is considered $R_\infty$-nilpotent if there exists a nilpotent subgroup of infinite height that intersects with every nilpotent subgroup of $G$. The degree of $R_\infty$-nilpotency in $G$ is then defined as the minimum height of nilpotent subgroups of $G$ that satisfy this condition. In this research, we investigate the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of various groups, such as direct products of groups, finitely generated groups, solvable groups, and torsion groups, where $R$ is a set of commutators. Additionally, we establish criteria and theorems related to the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of nilpotent and solvable groups.

A next-generation linear collider, either an e+e- collider or a muon collider, will offer the unique opportunity to precisely measure the top quark mass at a high level of accuracy. A test facility or a demonstrator project is essential to develop and validate the necessary instrumentation, algorithms, and methodology before embarking on this ambitious project. These components are crucial for successfully achieving the top quark mass measurement goal. In this study, we explore how a test project could be incorporated into an existing or planned program and propose either building a top quark factory or integrating top quark production lines into an existing facility such as the International Linear Collider (ILC) or the Future Circular Collider (FCC-ee). A top factory or the upgrade of the production lines would enable the simultaneous generation of multiple top quark pairs, allowing for a comprehensive top quark mass measurement with minimal statistical uncertainty within a relatively short period. In both scenarios, it's possible to incorporate both an e+e- collider and a muon collider test project, as well as an upgrade of the production lines at a cost significantly lower than building a full test facility.

In ultrafast experiments involving high-intensity lasers and atomic nuclei, researchers face significant challenges in extracting precise data due to noisy and intertwined experimental data. To overcome these issues, a novel inversion method centered around machine learning has been developed for extracting essential data from noisy and high-dimensional experimental data. This approach employs a modular architecture that incorporates multiple modules, each responsible for a specific physical aspect, and utilizes a universal K-fold strategy to account for various experimental conditions. Through simulations of practical experiments, the method demonstrates its ability to accurately recover important data from noisy and complex datasets within a relatively short time frame.

Using the Bag Model for light hadrons, researchers have long recognized the significance of Light-Cone Perturbation Theory in understanding the distribution amplitudes of various hadrons. More recently, this approach has been successfully applied to heavy light hadrons, allowing for a thorough comparison of heavy-light and light-heavy distribution amplitudes. Notably, studies found that heavy-light mesons tend to exhibit more symmetric quark distributions and, on average, lower momentum fractions than their light-heavy counterparts. To build upon this understanding, this work presents LCT calculations for the lightest $s$-charmed mesons and compares the distribution amplitudes of their corresponding pseudoscalar, vector, and axial-vector counterparts. Our findings indicate that, generally, these mesons' distribution amplitudes are less diverse and, relative to their $D$-series counterparts, exhibit a greater presence of $u$-quarks and, on average, lower momentum fractions. Moreover, when exploring the effects of radial excitations, we observe distinct trends in the distribution amplitudes of the $D^*_s$ meson series, which, unlike their $D$-series counterparts, demonstrate a more pronounced presence of $s$-quarks in the $D^*_{s2}(2573)$ and less diversity in the distribution amplitudes of the $D^*_s$ meson series compared to their $D$-series counterparts.

By expanding the existing growth estimate framework, we introduce a new pair of growth estimates, ${\tilde M}_1$ and ${\tilde M}_2$, where ${\tilde M}_1 (t) = M_1(t) l_{\alpha, \beta} (t)$ and ${\tilde M}_2 (t) = M_2(t) l_{\alpha, \beta} (t)^{1/2}$. Here, $l_{\alpha, \beta} (t) = e^{(\alpha + \beta / 2) t^2} (1 + \frac{\beta}{2} t^2)^{\alpha / 2}$, and the constants $\alpha$ and $\beta$ satisfy non-negative real values. We then establish the relationship between the growth estimates ${\tilde M}_1$ and ${\tilde M}_2$, and the Gelfand-Shilov spaces $G_{M_1, M_2, \alpha, \beta}^{(L)}$ and $G_{M_1, M_2, \alpha, \beta}^{(R)}$. Deep learning-based methods for cyberdarling instance segmentation have achieved significant performance improvements. However, they still face a fundamental challenge: the lack of a comprehensive cyberdarling dataset. This issue has led to the development of segmentation models that rely on synthetic data, such as MapBox-Studio, to produce satisfactory results. Nevertheless, using such an approach results in poorly defined object boundaries due to the inherent limitations of 2D mapping tools. This paper proposes an innovative solution called CySGAN, which builds on a Generative Adversarial Network architecture in conjunction with a 2D fully convolutional network, designed to generate high-quality instance segmentation in 3D point cloud formats. The proposed CySGAN approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy, speed, and generalizability on multiple datasets, including the widely used KITTI dataset. Moreover, it demonstrates superior performance on cyberdarling instance segmentation by leveraging its ability to create richly detailed output from sparse input.

In computer vision, action anticipation has gained significant attention as a crucial capability for autonomous systems to navigate uncertain environments. Recent approaches using Future of Action (ForA) networks have demonstrated impressive performance, but they are limited to geometric representations and ignore important spatial relationships. To address this, we introduce a novel ForA network that incorporates Spatial Temporal Graph (STG) using Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernels. The STG network leverages a kernel-induced graph structure, facilitating direct incorporation into the ForA framework. Our method surpasses the baseline ForA model in anticipation accuracy on JHMDB-21 and UCF101-24 actions, with an notable improvement of 8.9% and 12.3% respectively, when compared to models utilizing only geometric representations.

This study examines how H-alpha emission in stellar flares is affected by a variety of factors, including the intensity of the visible and far ultraviolet continuum, the ionization level of the gas, and the rate at which energy is released in the flare. To explore this, we analyzed data from the MINI-MEG and GUDMAP instruments on K2-185 B (a white hot star every 1.4 days) during a flare that occurred on March 20, 2020. We analyzed the spectrum of this flare because it was similar to other types of flares on hot stars, also known as FUor type III flares, which emit energy across the spectrum, particularly in the visible and far ultraviolet parts of the spectrum, causing the ionization of hydrogen and other elements to increase. We found that the ionization levels of hydrogen and other elements reached extremely high levels, over 10 to the power of 18 per square centimeter per second, during this flare. We used the least squares deconvolution method to separate out different emission lines in the flare and compared our results to other types of flares on hot stars, also known as FUor type II and III flares. We found that the ratio of H-alpha emission to the visible and far ultraviolet continuum emissions in this flare was similar to other types of flares on hot stars, also known as FUor type III flares.
