The coronavirus pandemic led to widespread media coverage, with news outlets emphasizing local perspectives. This research analyzed factors influencing the volume and content of local news regarding COVID-19, employing a Bayesian hierarchical model to combine national and provincial data from 81 Canadian provinces. Results demonstrated the significance of population size, provincial health crises, and national death rates in shaping local news coverage. Additionally, findings indicated that Sundays typically featured the lowest volume of news and that morning broadcasts prioritized health crisis management over economic concerns. With increasing provincial health crises, morning broadcasts shifted from emphasizing general news to COVID-19-related stories. By contrasting these patterns, this study offers insight into the dynamics governing the intersection of local media, public discourse, and public health policy during the pandemic.

To count infinity, you must be prepared to underwhelm yourself. The concept of systematic extrapolation in the limit of infinite data has its roots in the infinite hierarchy of Russell and Whitehead, where the property of interest is gradually defined. Following the success of applications like natural language processing and graph representation learning, systematic extrapolation has become a promising approach for countering data scarcity and model biases. Building on p-adic continuity and the Weisstein algorithm, we propose a novel method for extrapolating beyond the scope of finite datasets while ensuring convergence within an infinite data scenario. Moreover, this approach enables model selection without the constraints typically associated with limited datasets, thereby allowing for the choice of more computationally intensive models. As such, we model the likelihood of choosing a particular candidate model using the non-degenerate continuous analogue of the Blackwell-Dubins-Ferguson representation theorem.

Bloom filters employ cryptographic hash functions to identify potential set members, but they can suffer from false positives due to hash collisions. Xor filters, introduced by Herley and Probst, appear to offer a superior alternative, claiming both lower memory usage and faster lookup times compared to traditional Bloom filters. However, the proposed solution comes with its own set of limitations, including the necessity for modified hash functions and additional memory requirements for xor tables. In this research, we delve into the theoretical foundations of Xor filters, identifying both strengths and weaknesses, and revealing that, contrary to initial claims, Bloom filters may actually outperform Xor filters in certain scenarios. Specifically, we demonstrate the existence of hash functions for which the modified Bloom filter of a set has substantially less memory usage than the equivalent Xor filter. Moreover, we show that the assumed speed benefits of Xor filters are a result of misleading average-case analysis, and, in fact, lookup operations on Xor filters can be significantly slower than those on standard Bloom filters for a range of realistic workload scenarios. These findings underscore the importance of subjecting proposed optimizations to rigorous theoretical examination before advocating their adoption.

This article extends the Alexandrov body method from section 2 to the setting of (qP^N)s. It starts with the definition of a qP^N manifold, a geometric space that can be thought of as a (Q P^N)-manifold with weighted coordinates. For any big Q-divisor on a quasi-projective variety, X, the article develops a geometric construction, known as the Alexandrov body, which is associated with the numerical divisorial Zariski decomposition of X. The Alexandrov body's construction is initially considered in the context of a qP^N manifold and relevant mathematical properties, such as metric space properties, are applied to the numerical divisorial Zariski decomposition of X. The article also includes a case study of its application to 3-dimensional toric Fano manifolds.

This research suggests an efficient method for extracting market direction from reduced data sets, analyzing the time periods in which significant market movements occur. A study of the S&P 500 stock index from 2000 to 2019 used daily closing prices and transaction data to identify trends lasting one to 50 trading days. A complex network representing the relationships between companies was created using the daily price data, and the transfer entropy method was employed to measure the predictive value of each company for the index over various time horizons. An optimization process identified the most influential companies and the durations in which they provide directional information to the index. A statistical analysis validated the results and revealed that network structure and transaction data can effectively condense market information down to a manageable sample size.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called $\text{FLVoogd}$, a standard-free, federated unsupervised learning technique that allows multiple organizations to collaborate in forming protected classes without compromising sensitive personal information.
$\text{FLVoogd}$ utilizes a combination of techniques such as differential privacy and secure multiparty computation to create a reliable and trustworthy framework.
Our results show that $\text{FLVoogd}$ can successfully identify demographic classes in synthetic and real-world data sets, outperforming existing state-of-the-art unsupervised clustering methods.

Current autonomous vehicle development relies heavily on sim2real techniques to transfer policies from virtual to real-world environments. Despite these efforts, there is still a significant gap between performance in simulation and real-world results. This paper suggests that the problem lies not in the lack of advanced modeling techniques but rather in the unsuitable choice of evaluation metrics for sim2real transfer. These metrics often prioritize quantitative measures, such as speed and safety, over qualitative aspects, even though these qualities hold significant practical value in sim2real learning. To illustrate this point, the authors conducted the 2021 NEURIPS sim2real challenge, where 50 teams tested real-world autonomous driving policies derived from simulations. Notably, the winning team's policy, designed for a straightforward scenario, surprisingly worked relatively well in more complex conditions, underscoring the importance of qualitative metrics in sim2real learning. This challenge highlighted several challenges and areas for further research in autonomous driving, including the need for more realistic pedestrian models and more collaborative project structures that foster a sense of community among participants.

As the creation and dissemination of deepfakes intensify the risks and consequences for the public, there's an urgent need for automated deepfake detection tools. Researchers have made significant strides in developing deepfake detection systems, particularly neural network-based approaches, which have achieved remarkable accuracy in classifying media authenticity. However, these models are hindered by significant limitations, including substantial computational requirements, intricate model complexity, and a lack of transparent decision-making processes. To address these challenges, we propose a novel transformer-based architecture that leverages both global and local features from the input images to classify them as authentic or fake. This proposed model showcases exceptional performance on the two main deepfake benchmarks, CFAS-90v2 and FaceForeniscs++WF, outshining the current state-of-the-art models and requiring significantly fewer parameters and computational resources.

We utilized a planetary core and atmosphere model to investigate the diverse atmospheres on planets with masses between those of Earth and Neptune. Our research focused on 1.5 and 10 Earth masses as representative cases for small and massive atmospheres, respectively. We discovered distinct differences in the compositions and temperature profiles of these two types of atmospheres. In small atmospheres, carbon and nitrogen combined with oxygen to form CO and N$_2$O, while hydrogen and helium dominated the massive atmospheres. The loss of volatile elements in massive atmospheres led to extremely low surface pressures, ultimately resulting in negligible internal heat budgets and narrow temperature ranges. In contrast, small atmospheres experienced intense high- and mid-frequency UV radiation-driven escape, frequently leading to atmospheric loss exceeding the mass of the planet's core. We discovered that for massive atmospheres, pressure suffocated the faint ultraviolet radiation signal, while in small atmospheres, high surface pressures often masked a potentially significant signal of molecular hydrogen. Our models indicate that temperate planets with masses that significantly exceed our solar system's main-sequence star are unlikely to support life.

The McCulloch-Pitts network builds on the foundation of the classic Hopfield network and introduces a novel training method that utilizes local gradient backpropagation. This innovative approach enables the MCP network to learn nearly any target function, contrasting with the restrictive capabilities of traditional Hopfield networks. Notably, the MCP network's ability to learn is made possible by incorporating a dual set of neurons with distinct synaptic connections, one set trained via gradient backpropagation and the other operating under local hebbian plasticity. Interestingly, the mechanism by which local gradient propagation allows for the representation of complex, global patterns in the weight matrix remains poorly understood. To gain insight into this phenomenon, we developed a theoretical framework that illustrates how the incorporation of three key components - non-linearity, self-reinforcement, and backpropagation - contributes to the emergence of high-level abstractions in neural networks operating within local gradient dynamics.

Scene text recognition models have achieved significant advancements in recent years,
thanks in part to the rapid growth of the Oxford Towns dataset. This increase has
also led to a corresponding rise in Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) data, offering a means
to enhance existing models. In this study, we introduce the Oxford OOV Challenge,
a comprehensive platform centered on developing effective OOV data extraction and
utilization techniques for STR models. Our challenge incorporates three primary
tasks: extracting Oxford OOV data from real-world sources, integrating this data
into STR models, and improving their overall accuracy in handling unseen words
and characters. Our experimental results indicate that both data-driven and
model-driven approaches are essential in addressing the OOV challenge, and that
combined efforts from the research community are needed to overcome this persistent
issue.

The project Validated Numerics for Parameter-Dependent System of Differential Equations aims to address a pressing challenge in the field. When dealing with parameter-dependent systems, most analytical and computational methods are unable to distinguish between distinct solution branches that exist for various parameter values. Even with multiple initial conditions, identifying unique trajectories poses a significant hurdle. Our project focuses on overcoming this difficulty by exploring validated numerical methods that can efficiently identify and distinguish isolated solution branches in a parameter-dependent dynamic system. These solution branches are characterized by distinct invariants, which are identified using the first integrals of the system. Our approach utilizes the validated flow method to compute separate solution branches, which are then grouped into equilibrium sets based on distinct invariant trajectories. A key innovation of this project is the development of a novel hybrid approach that leverages both the validated flow method and a set elimination technique to compute distinct solution branches. Furthermore, our method does not require multiple initial conditions, making it highly efficient. Through application to multiple test cases, we have successfully demonstrated the efficacy of our proposed computational framework for identifying isolated solution branches in parameter-dependent dynamic systems.

This research proposes an efficient method to detect changes in real-time systems and isolate failures in resource-limited settings, effectively extending the capabilities of model checking to dynamic systems with unknown parameters and limited computational resources. The approach leverages an updated version of the PC algorithm, a well-established method for causal discovery, to identify system changes and incorporates model checking techniques for failure analysis in a modified MaxPlusAlgebraicPetriNet framework. To accommodate the constraints of model checking on real-time systems in the worst case, the method utilizes a dynamic window approach, limiting the analysis to the immediate system state. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach for detecting changes and isolating failures in various systems, outperforming a basic window-based method and requiring significantly less computational resources.

We conducted an analysis of the red giant branches within the dwarf galaxy candidates Gaia-Sausage Enceladus and Wukong/LMS-1 using a novel method incorporating stellar mass information from Gaia Data Release 2 and EDR3. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on color-magnitude diagrams, our method doesn't presuppose any information about the galaxies themselves, thereby yielding more accurate metal abundance estimates. For Gaia-Sausage Enceladus, we determined a metal abundance of -1.66 dex, with a 95% confidence interval ranging from -1.98 to -1.34 dex. We also calculated a mass for the galaxy of (3.00 +/- 0.45) x 10^9 solar masses, indicating that star formation likely persisted for approximately 10 billion years. In contrast, Wukong/LMS-1 exhibits a significantly higher metal abundance of -0.78 dex, with a 95% confidence interval spanning from -1.13 to -0.43 dex. We estimate the mass of Wukong/LMS-1 to be (0.43 +/- 0.07) x 10^9 solar masses. Notably, the metal abundance spread within both galaxies is substantial, suggesting a complex and intricate history of formation and evolution.

We establish that the homotopy orbit spectrum $(Z[[G]])_{hG}$ is topologically equivalent to the spectrum $Z$ when $G$ is a discrete group that possesses a subgroup with characteristics of a solvable abelian group. Additionally, we find the homotopy orbit spectrum for $G=\mathbb{Z}_2$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$, and apply these findings to the equivariant cobordism theory.

Machine learning models need labeled data to function accurately, but creating these labels can be time-consuming, expensive, and costly. A technique known as selective labeling tackles this issue by limiting the amount of data that needs to be annotated. In this approach, a trained model predicts data samples' relevance or class labels without requiring manual annotation, while unlabelled data is used to refine the model. This paper improves upon selective labeling by presenting a method called Searched Selective Labeling, which involves using search algorithms such as hill climbing, simulated annealing, and genetic algorithm to find the ideal set of data characteristics that produce the most accurate model. Experimental results on four real-world datasets show that Searched Selective Labeling outperforms other methods, including random selection, strategically selected features, and a novel algorithm called Data Characterization.

The computational model for the interface between EuS and InAs accurately describes the observed photoemission spectrum, but the analysis reveals that the significant dispersion at the top of the InAs valence band plays a crucial role in the interface's electronic structure. The dispersion results in the dispersion of InAs dipoles within the interface, which affects the photoemission spectrum. The interface's electronic structure is primarily determined by Eu 5d and InAs 4f states, but the significant dispersion alters this interpretation, suggesting that the primary benefit of considering the interface's quantum nature is to align the theoretical model with the experimental Photoemission Spectrum.

We establish a connection between continuous second-order arithmetic and infinite games of Borel Wadge, demonstrating that Borel Wadge determinacy implies a specific conjecture in the arithmetic. This relationship is analogous to a proven theorem by R.~S.~Fisher, which shows that projective determinacy has implications for true arithmetic. Our proof builds on concepts from high(er) degree logic and uses notions of interpretation to link concepts from logic with those of game theory. Furthermore, it presents an alternative framework for understanding concepts of Borel Wadge determinacy and projective determinacy, which may offer complementary insights to those previously proposed by Fisher and R.~M.~Gavalev.

Neural network pruning has effectively reduced the storage and computational costs associated with full models, but accurate distribution and batch resizing are crucial for processed models to achieve optimal performance. The issue with resizing batches is particularly prevalent in training environments where datasets cannot be modified. ClickTrain addresses this limitation by employing accurate batch resizing and training from the start with a modified cross-entropy loss, resulting in improved inference performance that surpasses traditional pruning methods when tested on the ImageNet dataset.

We establish a relational semantics for substructural modal logics by combining existing methods for each individual category (substructural and modal) and adapt the hypersequents method to model these complex logics, thereby providing a direct translation from sequent calculus to relational calculus.

The detection of binary neutron star mergers through multi-messenger observations has significant implications for astrophysics and cosmology. Future events, such as those from third-generation gravitational wave detectors like LIGO-V4 and VIRGO, including additional, improved sensors like KAGRA and the detectors at the upcoming DECIGO site, are expected to significantly expand our knowledge base. This will involve utilizing the full range of observational capabilities, from gravitational waves to electromagnetic radiation, to thoroughly analyze the mergers of neutron stars and black holes. By employing advanced machine learning techniques, researchers can optimize their search for these events, effectively reducing noise and increasing the detectors' sensitivity range. This will involve using the observed patterns in gravitational waves, such as their frequency ratios and tidal displacements, to guide the search for electromagnetic counterparts based on their sky positions, allowing for more targeted and efficient observations. Furthermore, by combining the capabilities of the gravitational wave and electromagnetic observatories, researchers can simulate various astrophysical scenarios on a large scale, mirroring the observations of the merging of neutron stars and black holes in the early universe. Ultimately, this will involve using the full range of observational capabilities to analyze the full spectrum of cosmic gravitational waves, from the short bursts detected in the gamma-ray band to the much longer waves detected in the nearly decoupled background.

The Jupiter-analogue planet, TOI-5542b, orbiting a G-dwarf star in the NGC 2616 molecular cloud, is an exceptional object for studying planetary composition and formation. Being a near-infrared bright planet, TOI-5542b can be analyzed using the JWST for its mid-level infrared spectrum, allowing the assessment of its atmospheric gas abundance, temperature profile, and structural characteristics. To examine the atmospheric structure of TOI-5542b, we applied a novel two-step forward modeling approach that incorporates a new algorithm, 'ATM' for atmospheric analysis. This new method efficiently generates atmospheric models and conducts convergence tests to ensure accuracy and reliability. Applying this approach to TOI-5542b's data from multiple instruments on both Earth and in space reveals that its best-fitting atmospheric model suggests a gas mixture composed of 0.57$\pm$0.14$F_{{\rm H}_2}$, 0.13$\pm$0.09$F_{{\rm He}}$, and various other less abundant gases, with an atmospheric scale height of 1000$\pm$200 km. Notably, our analysis detects very little water vapor in TOI-5542b's atmosphere. We observed that TOI-5542b's atmospheric composition and structure are consistent with a smooth, compact planet with no subsurface layers and a rock-iron core surrounded by a large gas envelope. Its mid-level temperature profile

This study presents a sampling-based primal-dual algorithm that generates a sustainable operation policy for complex decision-making problems with a convex resource constraint. Our approach capitalizes on the benefits of sampling and operation policy learning to enhance solving efficiency. We demonstrate that this algorithm is convergent and achieves a favorable convergence rate. In addition, we enhance the algorithm to accommodate static and dynamic scenarios with uncertain resources, and apply it to a power system with renewable energy sources. The results show that our method yields a significant reduction in computational cost, reaching up to a factor of 86.5, compared to conventional methods.

This study presents a method to automatically identify mathematical symbols in handwritten texts through a two-stage process. Firstly, a kNN classifier using handcrafted features detects symbols in isolated form. Subsequently, a contextual analysis module with a neural network integrates the results of the kNN classifier and generates symbol recognition data. This context analysis module is trained on data with manually annotated symbol connections, retrieved from the OpenMath dataset. To improve the reliability of the kNN classifier, it is retrained on a subset of data from the WISDOM dataset, specifically on images of symbols with superimposed random noise levels. This approach enables the system to process a wide range of mathematical expressions, utilizing a combination of handcrafted and neural features. Ultimately, our system demonstrates the feasibility of symbol recognition in complex mathematical expressions, achieving a high accuracy of 67% on the OpenMath dataset and 60% on the WISDOM dataset.

We examine the degeneracies of BPS states in four-dimensional black hole entropology. First, we expand the degeneracy formula by considering all points K configurations on the Hilbert scheme of C^2 and find its growth rate. This involves calculating an exponential index value which increases with K, contrasting its logarithmic index counterpart. Subsequently, we explore a new series of polynomials connected to the central charges of BPS states, defined for any N instantons. This series is represented by a sum of products containing K factors, where each product corresponds to a configuration of points K on the Hilbert scheme of C^2. We compute its leading terms and find a strong connection with the index degeneracy growth, explaining its own growth through the representation theory of a certain algebra. Finally, we outline possible applications of our findings, including extensions to M-theory and type IIA theory.

Understanding the spread of a disease within a population is a complex issue,
where certain factors, such as the population's interconnectedness and the rate at
which the disease is transmitted, contribute to its progression and impact. In this
study, we analyze epidemics in a population structure that is representative of
real-world environments, with a particular focus on their patterns of spread
and the factors that influence the outcome. Our findings indicate that the likelihood
of an epidemic is lower in highly interconnected populations and that a rapid rate
of transmission does not necessarily result in a severe outbreak. Rather, the outcome
is often characterized by a moderate number of infected individuals. In contrast,
a slow rate of transmission typically results in little to no impact. In general,
the likelihood of an epidemic is lower in highly interconnected populations and
can be predicted through a simple expression that incorporates the rate of transmission
and a measure of network connectivity, or "bridgeness."

We introduce an approach to reinforcement learning that incorporates safety considerations as probabilistic constraints. This novel methodology, called ProCon RL, utilizes conic approximations and dual optimization for efficient and exact compliance with safety constraints in reinforcement learning. As a significant advantage, ProRL can limit the incidence of safety breaches by a substantial factor, often from $10^3$ to $10^6$, and effectively boosts the success rate of training agents that adhere to critical system integrity. We apply this method in two challenging scenarios: navigating a robotic arm through a hazardous environment and achieving a goal in a restricted space, and achieve significant enhancements in success rates for these tasks.

We develop a twin prime identification method rooted in number theory, which focuses on the concept of twin primitivity based on specific number relationships rather than traditional combinatorial approaches. Our approach is grounded in the concept of 'twins' as pairs of numbers with a specific relative relationship, which can be applied broadly to identify twin primes by focusing on their unique generating factors. We explore the unique properties of twin primes within this framework, which enable the efficient generation of twin prime pairs. Our proposed algorithm is centered on the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, which provides a precise way to express numbers as products of prime numbers, allowing for the effective identification of twin primes through a systematic and predictable process.

We introduce a novel layered control system that navigates complex environments with sonar sensors on mobile platforms, achieving successful implementation on a quadcopter and a wheeled robot. These systems operate in dynamic settings with dynamic objects and reversible sound patterns, where we have developed a method to construct topological maps from sonar measurements. Our approach integrates expert knowledge to streamline the mapping process and enhance navigation. We demonstrate the efficacy of our layered control system through simulations and real-world experiments in various environments.

The low-resolution spectra obtained for Nereid in 2005 and 2006 using the Keck II telescope's LRiSS spectrograph revealed that its surface primarily composed of water ice, similar to other distant objects in the solar system. These spectra also showed Nereid's surface to have a complex and uneven composition, with multiple spectral features unable to be explained by standard models of solar system objects. The phenomenon of backward scattering was observed in both years, with Nereid's blue tail seemingly caused by physisorption photons. Notably, this phenomenon was more pronounced in 2005 when the sun and Nereid were aligned due to the orientation of its surface features. The observation of Nereid's surface morphology and its distant surroundings with the Hubble Space Telescope in 2005 provided evidence of small icy particles surrounding the moon, with their scattering behavior incompatible with standard scattering theory. The investigation of Nereid's properties offers a chance to gain insight into the satellite-moon interaction processes occurring when Neptune's moon Triton is perturbed from its stable ring system.

We examine projective planes formed by extending affine planes from the projective line over a ring, and we investigate how to merge these affine planes into a single projective plane. We provide conditions under which this merging is possible, and we explore the relationship between the order of the projective plane and the characteristics of the ring it's constructed from.

This note demonstrates the utility of the Tukey-order with models, introducing novel relationships between cardinal characteristics such as $	om_n$ and $	om_{	om_n}$, and providing a framework for comparing general instances of uncountable cardinal properties. Specifically, it showcases the method's effectiveness in establishing the consistency of certain positive relationships between these characteristics, and its potential use in proving positive results, particularly those involving large cardinal concepts.

We integrate the pessimism principle into Thompson sampling to enhance the efficiency of optimizing dynamic treatment policies. This results in a posterior maximization algorithm known as POM TS, which makes fewer assumptions than current pessimistic algorithms while maintaining posterior concentration locally around its global maximum. We theoretically demonstrate that POM TS reaches a superior local maximum compared to conventional Thompson sampling, and our empirical analysis reveals that POM TS outperforms its pessimistic counterpart on a variety of bandit and medical intervention scenarios.

Given a finitely generated module $M$ over a connective ring with $K$-theory, we identify the lowest-level subcategory of modules that splits off from $K$-theory for larger-sized modules. This subcategory is characterized by modules with vanishing $K$-theory. This subcategory's invariance directly impacts Algebraic $K$-theory extensions for larger-sized modules. Similar results hold for Quillen's $K$-theory for exact categories.

We examine the connections between distinct quantum state configurations in Bell and Jaynes-Cumming models, utilizing a novel conceptual framework. Our analysis reveals that these connections can be understood through a combination of nonlocality and contextuality in the Bell case, and pure state correlations in the Jaynes-Cumring model. Furthermore, applying the concept of equivalence between configurations allows us to establish relationships between nonlocality and contextuality and pure state correlations, thereby providing a unified explanation for the identical outcomes in Bell and Jaynes-Cumming experiments.

In this study, we examine etapairing in multi-band Hubbard models, featuring nested fermionic pseudoparticles and an etapairing symmetry characteristic. By constructing exact etapairing ground states through analytic methods, we overcome reliance on quantum Monte Carlo simulations for these models. Our results show that etapairing is strongest at filling =p/q = 1/3, with shorter-range pairing emerging at 1/2 filling. The d-wave pairing of the two-band Hubbard model models this in the idealized limit of separate orbital energies, distinct from our generalised $eta$-pairing scenario.

We investigate the analog of the generalized P\'olya theorem within the framework of A-adic solenoids. This involves using continuous A-adic functions to solve a novel functional equation. By leveraging properties of the d'Alembertian equation and Cauchy's functional equation, we can reduce the problem to a manageable task. Along the way, we derive a distinctive formula for the product of two A-adic values, which showcases the complexities of the A-adic number system.

Presence-absence data, commonly employed in ecological studies, have variables that follow a binary distribution. Due to its sparsity, this type of data poses significant challenges for clustering, leading researchers to employ specialized methods such as binary partitioning, hard or soft clustering, and predictive models. Recently, neural networks have gained prominence in data analysis, yet previous work has highlighted issues with their efficacy on sparse data. To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework, SpikeNet, for clustering sparse presence-absence data. SpikeNet capitalizes on the capabilities of multilayer perceptrons by incorporating a spike activation function and data augmentation. To improve model robustness, we applied two techniques: a regularization layer and early stopping. Through comprehensive evaluation of our approach on 60 datasets from the PASCAL2 benchmark, we have found that SpikeNet surpasses existing methods in terms of clustering performance, achieving notable improvements in 74% of the datasets and comparable results to state-of-the-art methods in the remaining cases.

The emergence of RGB-D cameras like Kinect has significantly impacted video gaming and human-computer interaction by providing detailed, three-dimensional visual data. However, converting these depth maps into usable numerical values can be time-consuming, especially when combining depth and color information to pinpoint key objects. Traditionally, depth maps are converted into binary masks, then combined with color channels, before being processed by advanced networks. This labor-intensive and inefficient method not only prolongs computation time but also limits the accuracy of object detection algorithms. To address these limitations, we've developed a unified structure that seamlessly integrates color and depth features, thereby speeding up processing time and achieving higher precision. The proposed approach, called Uniswap, utilizes dual convolutional layers to fuse color and depth data, then feeds the combined features into a unified transnasal block, which extracts distinctive features and accurately detects objects. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques on the MS-COCO, PASCAL Context, and DDD datasets, also achieving up to a 20% increase in accuracy on certain datasets.

This research focuses on detecting abusive content in social media by identifying
toxic language in tweets, utilizing a dataset developed by IBM. The study explores
two approaches: a standalone model and a combination of features, which are then
utilized to test a proposed architecture utilizing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
neural networks. The results demonstrate that an LSTM network with a macro F1 score
of 0.77 on the IBM dataset outperforms a supporting model, which achieves a macro
F1 score of 0.74. The selected model was then submitted to the IBM Watson competition, where it ranked 11th among 21 competing systems.

Consider an integer representation system defined by an irrational rotation of the circle, where α and β are distinct irrationals satisfying a specific condition, and let P be a palindromic number in this representation system. We establish that the majority of integers within a large, circumscribed range cannot be expressed as P divided by their greatest common divisor with a positive integer q.

We present a novel data-driven method for 3D X-ray Computed Tomography (CT) image reconstruction that can adapt to various types of input noise. To achieve this, our model utilizes a generative adversarial network (GAN) framework, which produces high-quality, noise-free images while learning from noisy, real data. By integrating a noise estimation network, our model becomes robust to different noise levels and sources. As a result, our method outperforms conventional low-dose CT reconstruction techniques in both low-dose and ultra-low-dose CT scans, as confirmed by experimental data.

Deep neural networks can recreate programs in symbolic domains such as handwriting, but their capacity is limited to specific scenarios. A more robust approach, Bayesian Program Learning, extracts a probabilistic program that resembles the expert's method, using numerous samples and without assuming the program structure or inputs/outputs relationships. We've successfully applied BPL to generate handwriting, an inherently complex task, and the results show that this method produces more varied and accurate outputs than traditional machine learning, using many orders of magnitude fewer samples. Furthermore, the program's coefficients have significant correlations with the expert's, indicating that BPL captures the underlying rules of the handwriting program. Additionally, the probabilistic nature of BPL allows us to draw samples of new characters, by propagating uncertainty through the program.

A newly created computational framework, known as the ThreeNucleonInteraction, enables the efficient generation of three-nucleon interaction matrix elements for quantum chemistry and chemistry methods. This resource builds upon prior efforts, like the MNDCdb database, by integrating data from multiple sources: the MNDCdb, the ENDF/FX database, and ChaoKuLiu's research findings. A novel storage approach, based on graph theory, significantly reduces the memory required to store the interaction data. Compared to traditional methods, this framework reduces memory requirements by a factor of 10 to 1000 times, making it more suitable for use with next-generation quantum computers.

The advent of quantum electronics has created a pressing need to extend traditional electrical engineering techniques to quantum systems. Achieving this goal hinges on a deep understanding of the quantum circuit framework. Two key concepts in this framework are the correlator method and the von-Neumann density-matrix method, both centered around the exploration of entanglement. Notably, these methods excel in analyzing hybrid quantum-classical systems, leveraging the principles of Green functions and Kadanoff-Baym equations. By applying these concepts, researchers can gain profound insights into the fundamental properties of quantum devices, paving the way for groundbreaking advancements in quantum electronics.

Let D be a bounded convex domain in C-d dimension (d is less than or equal or to 3). Assume that the boundary of D contains non-trivial analytic discs. In this paper, we will provide criteria to determine if a composition operator defined on the space of holomorphic functions on D is compact or not.

We've derived the two-loop anomalous dimensions of several key twisted-conformal operators of weight four in the SU(2) global symmetry series, which governs the dynamics of multiple, massless fermions scattered across a one-dimensional interval in a specific framework known as the AdS/CFT correspondence. This framework is used to study a system of multiple, massless bosons in a one-dimensional space called the sausage, which is used to calculate various physical properties such as structure factors and form factors for this system. Calculations of these corrections are complex and require an understanding of the interplay between two-loop corrections and the principles of caustic formation in this system.

Most high-performance GPU applications rely on memory allocators to manage memory usage, but the standard allocator frequently results in memory fragmentation, wasting valuable GPU memory and slowing down applications. In order to address this issue, we developed DynaSOAr, a sophisticated, parallel memory allocator that efficiently manages memory on GPUs with high efficiency. By employing a combination of cyclic memory allocation and smart memory management, including the use of overlapping memory blocks and merging adjacent free memory regions, DynaSOAr minimizes memory fragmentation and runs at a very low overhead. In comparison to the standard memory allocator, DynaSOAr reduces memory fragmentation by a factor of 100 to 1000 times, resulting in a 10 to 100 times increase in allocation speed, and in certain tests, even matches the performance of the optimal, static allocator.

We investigate the possibility of isospin violation in dark matter detection, taking into account two specific models of U(1)X theories. Isospin violation can occur due to the difference in dark current masses or Lienard-Cowan factors. Our analysis reveals that, in both models, isospin violation significantly reduces the cross-section at high-energy reactors like the one at BERII. This reduction helps evade current experimental limits from the BERII experiment. Consequently, the U(1)X models with massless mediator and dark matter become more compatible with existing dark matter abundance requirements, as their unitriaxial isotropic isotropy structure prevents conflict with big-bang relic abundance limits at high-energy scales.

To create a tube's pre-tension based on its material properties, diameter, and wall thickness, it's crucial to remove any existing tension before the vacuum pressure becomes a consideration. A method has been established to evacuate an aluminum tube past its critical pressure point without compromising its structural integrity. Photographic and acoustic analysis enable the detection of even minute changes in the tube's shape. By studying these changes, we determined the minimum pre-tension required for straw tubes with a 10 mm diameter, which is a standard size used in various experiments, such as the NA62 and future precision physics projects. Based on these findings, we calculated the pre-tension needed for 10 mm and 50 mm long straw tubes to be approximately 20 MPa and 5 MPa, respectively. Notably, pre-tension falls within the 5-10% range recommended by CERN. Additionally, we demonstrate that a specific straw tube handling technique, which involves slowly inserting a rod into one end while supporting the other, enables successful tension measurement and allows for the removal of existing tension, ultimately allowing straw tubes to be designed without initial pre-tension.

We propose a method for assessing the reliability of decision functions in situations where there's uncertainty about how the decision rule will be evaluated. Our approach defines a metric for robustness and provides an approximation of this metric by treating specific aspects of the decision rule as variables. This approximation forms the basis of a convex optimization problem, the solution to which identifies the minimum and maximum possible robustness values. Crucially, these bounds enable us to compare the robustness of different decision functions in scenarios with uncertain parameters. To illustrate the utility of our framework, we examine a series of simple decision-making problems in areas such as, predictive modeling and adversarial testing, and show how it can be extended to handle more complex scenarios with additional constraints.

The nature of the solid structure in a supersolids is often studied through analysis of phonon modes near the roton minimum, and our research reveals that impurities with oscillatory movement within these modes can indicate supersolidity without necessarily producing soft modes. By applying a theory that accounts for long-range interactions in solid structure, we have found that impurities can shift the location of the roton minimum and alter the speed of sound in phonons, and this effect is most significant in systems where impurities make up a large percentage of the total particles. Our analysis also demonstrates that, in the presence of oscillating impurities, the suppression of superfluidity is characterized by a distinct shift in the divergence point of the superfluid density below a certain threshold percentage of impurities.

A subcode of a projective line arrangement in a generalized quadrangle is termed a neighbour-transitive code if it remains unchanged under permutations of adjacent points. We establish in this paper that a neighbour-transitive code in a quadrangle W is essentially a direct product code comprising two lines from W, each having a full linear coding over a prime field.

The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) is a critical area of study due to its connection with the Milky Way's central black hole and the anisotropy it influences.  Moving forward, researchers will focus on understanding the origin of the CMZ's intricate density patterns.  Past studies revealed significant density fluctuations on different scales, but there was debate over whether these patterns indicate the densest regions surround the central black hole or if they are simply the result of varying molecular gas density inclusion.  To address this, a team analyzed a detailed, three-dimensional density structure map of the CMZ, constructed using data from radio recombination line observations, for its radial and longitudinal patterns.  By examining how at densities vary with distance from the central black hole and how at varying at densities change with distance from the central black hole, researchers discovered that the densest regions surround the central black hole and that the central black hole influences the densest regions.  Furthermore, anisotropy in the densest regions changes with the scale.  CMZ density structure and its connection to the central black hole and the spiral arms of the galaxy.

We examined how using an X-ray free-electron laser affects the distribution of electrons in a target, using both experimental and computational methods to investigate a specific case of nickel. Results indicate that altering the initial electron configuration leads to significant differences in how the material absorbs the laser, with non-linear effects exhibiting a more pronounced change at higher fluences when the electron distribution is altered. This finding has far-reaching implications for high-field physics, suggesting that purposefully manipulating the initial electron state could lead to enhanced outcomes in various experiments.

A highly accurate temperature sensor was developed using standard components found in most laboratories, excluding high-precision equipment. The design relies on a precise measurement of the thermal expansion of a resistive material, achieving exceptional accuracy thanks to a sophisticated compensation technique that accounts for subtle thermal coefficient variations in standard resistors. The sensor's high resolution and accuracy rival those of high-end digital thermometers, making it an invaluable asset for temperature control in scientific applications.

A combination of quantum scissors technique and conditional functions enables the preparation of complex entangled states in a system of polarized photons. We offer an alternative method using the Jaynes-Cummings cavity model which enables the production of two-photon entanglement through a single cavity. Our method avoids relying on non-permanent entities and instead utilizes a controlled input of coherent states. We outline a procedure for isolating two-photon states using the quantum scissors technique in both horizontal and vertical polarizations. This method can be expanded to prepare multi-photon entangled states by incorporating additional input coherent states.

The minimum spanning tree and minimum k-point spanning tree problems have been extensively studied in the online setting, with a significant focus on how the competitive ratio changes with the dimension. Interestingly, when it comes to forming a spanning tree with at most k points, the optimal online algorithm has a competitive ratio of O(log k), regardless of the dimension. In contrast, for general k-point spanning trees, the best online algorithm has a competitive ratio of O(log k / log log k) in dimensions two and three, and O(log k) in dimensions four and above. For d-dimensional Euclidean spaces and general k-point spanning trees, we present an online algorithm with a competitive ratio of O(log k) and allow up to k points as part of the solution. Specifically, our algorithm finds a k-point set that forms a beta-approximation of a given set of points. If a Steiner point is allowed as part of the solution, we present an online algorithm with a competitive ratio of O(log k) / (d + log k). Our approach demonstrates that limiting the number of points that can be added online does not inherently restrict the competitive ratio, even in higher dimensions.

As IoT devices continue to evolve, identifying them becomes increasingly vital. When categorizing devices, some scenarios may involve uncertain cases that lack clear identification as risks accompany misclassification. Given that IoT devices often harbor sensitive information, a misclassification could pose a threat to security. This paper addresses the challenge of accounting for risks in categorizing IoT devices during classification tasks, including an illustrative case study using the Malawi IoT dataset to demonstrate the techniques. Researchers developed a cost-aware classification approach, incorporating a risk model to minimize misclassification errors. This method leverages the context of resource-constrained IoT devices and provides a practical solution for tackling misclassification risks in real-world applications, as demonstrated by the accompanying code and data.

This paper provides a comprehensive classification of finite G\"odel algebras within the category of finite forest dendroids, establishing a duality between the two entities. Building upon this foundation, we explore specific subcategories of finite G\"odel algebras, including those comprising balanced, pseudo-Boolean, and semi-Boolean structures. Central to our inquiry is the relationship between these algebras and respective subcategories of finite forest dendroids, ultimately enabling us to calculate the cardinalities of sets involved.

This research explores a novel approach to learning aligners for languages that don't have rich resources, using a parameter-sharing strategy and unsupervised alignment techniques. Our results show that a trainer on a small corpus of data achieves comparable performance to established aligners, such as GIZA++ and Google's Translate tool. We also discovered that our approach is at least 20 times faster than traditional aligners. Furthermore, our unsupervised alignment method is significantly more effective than previously established methods. Due to its efficiency and effectiveness, we've made our aligner available as an alternative to existing aligners for languages with limited resources.

The performance of many scientific simulations heavily relies on the implementation of asynchronous communication protocols, which are often based on complex mathematical concepts such as tensor-structured data transfer models. Disentangling the challenges associated with synchronous and asynchronous simulations is crucial for developing efficient emulation techniques. This study introduces an asynchronous protocol for emulating the synchronous communication pattern in block-iterative algorithms utilizing quantum computing resources. Specifically, a detailed implementation of the asynchronous block-iterative decomposition algorithm based on quantum computation is presented, along with an examination of its underlying mathematical structure. Which involves application of the quantum QHJT and QGHJ algorithms to achieve computational goals. Furthermore, a thorough analysis of the algorithm's process is conducted to evaluate its computational and memory requirements. Ultimately, the asymptotic runtime complexity of the algorithm is found to be no more than O(N^(2/3) |L|^(1/3) T).

Future surveys at the Southern Sky are expected to significantly expand our knowledge of micro-lensing events caused by black holes and neutron stars. Predictions for such events have been made under the assumption that a significant portion of these detections will reveal evidence for primordial black holes, which could account for a large majority of the micro-lensing events observed. The simulations also take into account the contribution of stellar black holes and other compact objects such as neutron stars to aid in the understanding of the potential cosmological implications of these detections. The simulations show that if a typical primordial black hole mass is around 30 solar masses, predictions for the number of micro-lensing events caused by these objects far outweigh the number of such events caused by stellar objects. However, if the mass of these primordial black holes is lower, at around 8 solar masses, the predictions for the number of such events caused by these objects is similar to the number of such events caused by stellar objects. The simulations show that in order to determine the mass of these primordial blackholes, it will be necessary to detect over a hundred thousand micro-lensing events of these objects, which will require a large amount of data, which may not be necessary if a lower mass range for these blackholes is confirmed.

This study introduces a two-dimensional model of interacting hard disks that defines a one-dimensional variable representing disk position along a straight line. Based on this variable, two new frustrated polar crystalline phases are discovered, which emerge at a density higher than 0.5. In addition to these novel phases, we re-examined the parameter spaces for polar and monopolar systems and confirmed the long-held assumption that there are no more than two frustrated polar crystalline phases. Our analysis also demonstrates that the transition between these phases is of the Kosterlitz-Thouless type.

This research investigates how multiple applications of classical operations like differentiation and integration impact the positive definiteness of zonal functions. We demonstrate that even with a single integration, positive definiteness can be maintained. Conversely, differentiating a zonal function repeatedly will inevitably result in a function with non-positive definiteness. We also examine the implications of maintaining positive definiteness on bandlimited functions, both with and without restrictions on frequency content.

Quantum imaging has emerged as a key quantum technology, enabling us to obtain detailed insights into delicate specimens without causing any physical interaction. The implementation of phase-flip errors in this process, however, hinders our ability to obtain precise images. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel error correction method for quantum imaging. This approach utilizes a series of free-space laser pulses to correct errors in imaging fragile samples. Notably, our technique can be applied to the post-processing of images obtained through various experimental methods, including the interaction-free technique and others. To illustrate the efficacy of this error correction method, we have successfully implemented it in the context of imaging a Mach-Zehnder interferometer's output, achieving a high FQI value of 5.11 dB.

A liquid foam's surface texture and the particles adhering to it determine to what extent liquid can penetrate and flow through the foam. This study focuses on a specific type of fluid flow through a complex network of bubbles arranged in a specific pattern, and we examine how the "roughness factor" affects the fluid flow through the foam. This parameter characterizes the surface irregularities and influences the type of fluid flow through the foam. Using advanced mathematical equations, we investigated how changes in the "roughness factor" affect the fluid's viscosity and pressure within the foam. Our analysis shows that as the "roughness factor" increases, the fluid's viscosity and pressure within the foam also increase, and we observed a transition from one type of fluid behavior to another, all while maintaining a consistent ratio of surface tension to flow rate.

Deep learning techniques, specifically Ensemble Methods, combine multiple models to improve performance and coverage. This study focuses on the application of Ensemble Methods to 2D image classification using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), where recent advancements have seen significant improvements. To investigate how ensemble classifiers contribute to performance, this work undertakes a comprehensive analysis of an industrial X-ray image dataset, examining the variability in ensemble outcomes and their correlation with dataset characteristics. Based on these findings, two novel ensemble strategies are developed to optimize results, one selecting subsets of images and the other choosing portions of the CNN architecture. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that these ensemble approaches enhance the already superior base CNN results, achieving a maximum accuracy of 97.78% and 97.66% for the image classification of industrial defects and material identification, respectively.

To investigate how strongly electronically excited states in solid sodium interact with phonons, we considered the influence of long-range forces beyond nearest neighbors. Using first-principles calculations, we found that dipolar excitations of electron-hole pairs amplify the effect by a factor of 3, while monopole interactions remain within the expected range. The significant enhancement by the dipolar electron-hole excitation is caused by an almost linear relationship between the electron and hole positions. This significant increase in interaction also causes a significant dispersion of the phonon spectrum, with some phonon frequencies increasing by as much as 30% and others decreasing by as much as 20%. This level of detail in the phonon spectrum is essential for understanding the behavior of sodium at extremely high pressures.

We investigate the concept of work in microstates from a probabilistic perspective, where the concept of dissipated work, tied to thermodynamic systems, is reexamined. Traditionally, dissipated work is considered to be the energy lost by a system to the environment due to its initial and final states. However, this conventional definition appears to be at odds with the fundamental principles of reversible classical mechanics. Instead, we propose an alternative definition, asserting that the work done by a microstate is solely a manifestation of its internal dynamics. Consequently, the concept of dissipated work can be reinterpreted as the difference between the work done by a system in its initial and final states. Notably, this reinterpretation is consistent with the principles of reversible classical mechanics. Moreover, the reinterpretation also aligns with the principles of time-reversal in quantum mechanics.

This research establishes a method for calculating curvature weights in the cotangent bundle of a symplectic manifold, leading to a more intricate computation compared to standard Riemannian structures. As a result, this new formula may provide opportunities for new insights and challenges within the field of symplectic geometry.

We examine nonadiabatic acoustic waves in diatomic Hertzian chains where the discreteness plays a crucial role. In particular, we consider two scenarios: compressive chains with negative Hertzian potential and rarified chains with positive Hertzian potential. For both cases, we start with an asymptotically small parameter $\epsilon$ that governs nonadiabatic effects, and we find that to the order of $\epsilon^2$, the nonadiabatic perturbation is negligible and the motion is freely precessing. However, this change becomes more pronounced as $\epsilon$ decreases, and at the next order, the nonadiabatic correction splits into two contributions: a exponentially small oscillatory component and a constant error term. In the compressive chain, these oscillatory components cancel out, leading to a complete loss of precession, and the formation of solitary waves. In the rarified chain, the oscillatory components cancel out for diatomic chains with equal masses, but lead to a different behavior in ditomic chains with unequal masses.

In models of inflation featuring sharp features at field values, model-specific characteristics are preserved, whereas their amplitudes and locations are influenced by different physical parameters. This study evaluates the impact of these features on the observable signs of primordial non-Gaussianities within a specific class of inflationary models. Our findings demonstrate that the strongest, model-independent non-Gaussian signals emerge from scenarios where the feature's location aligns with the feature field value, and a particular, negative bispectrum configuration is matched. Additionally, we identify a distinct scenario in which the GP correction and the cubic non-linear interaction equally contribute to the primordial non-Gaussian forecast, a phenomenon observed only within this specific class of sharp feature models.

The Accordion Graph Class $A[n,k]$ consists of graphs where the vertex set can be divided into $k$ subsets, each representing a circle with $n$ vertices, and two vertices are connected if their corresponding circles match and contain a common segment of size $n-1$. A circulant graph is defined by a set of vectors that cover all vertices. We determine the conditions under which $A[n,k]$ is not a circulant graph and establish the minimum number of vectors required to construct a circulant $A[n,k]$.

We have developed and analyzed a quantum walk model based on aperiodic Markov processes, specifically examining the conditions under which periodic discrete-time quantum walks become dissipative quantum Weyl maps on certain groups of points. Our study reveals that, in these periodic discrete-time quantum walks, the rate of participant engagement remains consistently high even near the point of transition out of periodic motion, where the influence of randomness peaks. To better understand this behavior, we created numerical models representing walks on two types of settings: a finite line without boundaries and a finite circle with boundaries. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of increasing walk periods and found that the concentration of probability at the origin in the group's topological structure remains consistently high, provided that the period of the walk remains a prime number. We have expressed the final probability distribution at the origin in terms of the $t$th Fibonacci number, specifically for walks on a finite line without boundaries. In addition, we have used mathematical induction to demonstrate that the rate of participant engagement in these walks increases in a geometric progression, especially for walks on a finite circle with boundaries.

DINO, a self-supervised learning technique, has recently gained popularity for its effectiveness in fine-tuning Vision Transformers with minimal computational costs. DINO's ability to match or even surpass the performance of well-established supervised methods when utilizing two projection heads has made it particularly appealing. However, our investigation reveals that incorporating a dual-encoder architecture, which is a fundamental component of DINO, significantly hinders the performance of Vision Transformers when employing fewer projection heads. Conversely, incorporating a dual-encoder setup in conjunction with two projection heads fails to enhance the model's capabilities. We demonstrate that replacing the dual-encoder architecture in DINO with a self-supervised variant of the European BLSTM auto-encoder can significantly improve the model's performance on the ImageNet dataset. Specifically, our modifications yield a relative improvement of over 1 percentage point in the top-1 accuracy while reducing the computational costs by approximately 16.5% compared to the standard DINO implementation using two projection heads.

This study introduces an unconventional cosmological model where the viscosity coefficient $\eta$ is directly tied to the scale factor $a$, with $\eta \propto a^\nu$. The model is further developed by taking the anisotropy factor $\Gamma$ to be a function of time, resulting in interesting findings, including a dust-dominated era in the far future of the universe and potentially multiple matter-dominated phases. The study also examines the consequences of $\Gamma$ being a constant multiple of the Hubble parameter $H$ and explores the implications for the deceleration parameter $j$ and the effective viscosity coefficient $\bar{\eta}$ in relation to the scale factor $a$.

This study examines the ill-posedness of the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations in high-dimensional spaces with low-dimensional time domains. Specifically, we have found that in dimensions of $d\geq 2$ and for a time domain of $t\in\mathbb{R}^+,0<\alpha\leq 2-\frac{\sqrt{1+4\alpha^2}}{2}$, the Cauchy problem becomes ill-posed in the sense of non-solution existence in the Besov space $B_{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^d)$. Moreover, we have further proven that in dimensions of $d\geq 2$, and for a time domain of $t\in(0,1), 0<\alpha\leq 2-\frac{\sqrt{1+4\alpha^2}}{2}$, the Cauchy problem becomes highly unstable.

Artist.  Stable Artist is a user-friendly interface for creating artistic images, allowing individuals without artistic talent to contribute to the image generation process.  By incorporating a stylized prompt, users can produce unique images.  The system leverages Stable Diffusion to generate images, utilizing a combination of pre-trained models.  The interface offers several innovative features, including a control panel that enables users to adjust parameters, such as adjusting the strength of artistic style or color palettes, and a saved artwork gallery that enables users to access and manipulate previously created images.  The Artist can be accessed at stableartist.com.

Deep learning models are now predominantly trained using frequentist methods despite the inherent uncertainty in measurements and labeling errors that necessitate probabilistic approaches. We apply Bayesian techniques to quantify uncertainty in deep learning model choices, specifically in a scenario where multiple models are trained on varying datasets and testing scenarios. We develop a framework that treats model selection as a statistical hypothesis testing problem, enabling the calculation of a probability of error in predicting model superiority. This method is applied to two real-world problems, the selection of best practices in deep learning and the choice of data augmentation techniques, and successfully identifies the most probable models based on the proposed error rates.

We explore theoretical limits on dark matter particles interacting with nucleons through various mesons, based on observed limits on dark matter-nucleon cross sections by LUX-Zeplin and Xenon1t. Our analysis focuses on two decay processes: $J/\psi$ into invisible particles and into dark photons, with form factors modeled after those used in charmonium decays. By accounting for uncertainties in form factors and parton distribution functions, we derive tighter constraints on dark matter particles interacting with nucleons via $\rho$, $\omega$, and $A_1$ mesons. For example, our analysis reveals a $10^{-10}$ picobarn limit on the dark matter-cross section for a $A_1$ mediating dark matter-nucleon scattering.

Magnetic bright points (MBPs) are magnetically intense features that appear as bright spots in images of the solar surface. To study their properties, researchers analyzed over 2,500 MBPs, each with a magnetic field intensity of more than 1100 Gauss, from a dataset of polarimetric images, taken with the New Solar Telescope at Big Bear Solar Observatory, using an automated detection algorithm. The dataset included 315,000 pixels with a magnetic field intensity above 100 Gauss, making up about 0.6% of the total pixels in the dataset. The study found that the distribution of the solar surface area occupied by these features follows a power law with two parameters, while the distribution of their magnetic field intensities is bi-modal. The curvature of the magnetic field vectors in the MBPs was found to be more pronounced than in surrounding areas with weaker magnetic fields, with a median curvature of 0.014 arcsec^-1. The curvature distribution follows a power law, with the slope depending on the field strength. The study also found that the components of the velocity vector observed in the MBPs follow a normal distribution, while the components of the velocity vector observed in areas with magnetic field intensities just below the detection threshold follow a power law. The distribution of the components of the velocity vector observed in areas with magnetic field intensities above the detection threshold is not as well understood and requires further study.

Minimalistic videos showcasing diverse human movements would greatly benefit visual comprehension and recognition abilities. Currently, generating video human bodies from a single image receives attention, but creating coherent video sequences of human heads or full bodies remains an underinvestigated area. To address this, we propose a method called ProtoRNN, which utilizes a recurrent neural network to generate video sequences of human bodies. We then test our ProtoRNN framework on two challenging problems, one being the creation of minimalistic video clips from a single image and the other being the synthesis of video clips from a text description. Our ProtoRNN method excels in both tasks, outperforming existing approaches in a wide range of metrics and produces the most realistic video sequences at high speeds. Furthermore, to facilitate research in human video generation, we introduce a new dataset called ProtoRNN, which consists of a large collection of video clips in the format of MP4.

We investigated the properties of a non-Abelian gauge theory in its fully confined phase. This phase transition is caused by a deformation of SU(2) Yang-Mills theory through a non-Abelian Coulomb branch. We conducted this study using the holographic dual of this deformation, an asymptotically Anti-de Sitter space with three charged probes. These probes represent bound monopole ground states which transition as the external magnetic field changes. We discovered that within this fully confined phase, the monopole ground states exhibit a transition similar to a Sine-Glauian transition as the magnetic field strength changes. This behavior is characterized by a change from a state with a single, stable ground state to a state containing multiple ground states and a degenerate point.

Normalizing a dataset is a fundamental step in machine learning model training, yet its impact on subsequent model evaluations is frequently overlooked. This study investigates the effect of normalizing a large dataset of weather forecasts on the performance of subsequent machine learning models. Despite train-normalization not significantly influencing model accuracy, the study finds that testing models on unnormalized data yields more consistent and generalizable results. Consequently, the research suggests that removing normalizing transformations entirely may be a more effective approach than train-test split normalization for improving weather forecasting model outcomes.

We've investigated the LHC's capacity to detect dark matter in a specific class of three-Higgs-doublet models that incorporate CP violation. These models produce a distinctive signature - same-sign WW production - which can serve as a indicator for dark matter. Our analysis indicates that, in the presence of CP violation, the mass range of dark matter candidates is constrained to less than 2 TeV. Furthermore, we found that, without considering dark matter, the LHC can still establish a lower bound of 1.5 TeV on the mass of these candidates. Moreover, the models feature a naturally generated small PMNS phase, $\delta$, as a result of the strong CP violation, which aligns with experimental findings within the 1 sigma margin of error.

We investigate the PPT square conjecture in infinite dimensions. We demonstrate that in infinite dimensions, the PPT square property is consistent with separability. We also establish that in infinite dimensions, the PPT square property is consistent with the presence of pure states that are mutually perpendicular.

The transport of materials within neurons is influenced by the efficiency of microtubule structure and properties. Research has shown that certain types of neurotoxic proteins can bind to microtubules and cause them to become twisted and fragmented, affecting cellular transportation efficiency. A study has found that certain proteins, including those causing prion disease, can alter microtubule properties by changing the L/A ratio, leading to changes in cellular transportation efficiency. Utilizing finite element analysis, researchers simulated the effects of these proteins on microtubule properties and discovered that even small changes can cause fragmentation, leading to changes in transportation efficiency.

In the realm of banking and fraud detection, identifying fraudulent transactions within a customer's account requires analysis of their transaction history. This can be accomplished by examining the temporal relationships between transactions, which are represented as a directed graph. However, generating feasible and potentially fraudulent graphs within this framework poses a significant challenge. Most existing algorithms create unrealistic and invalid temporal graph models by omitting unconnected transactions or connecting unrelated ones, which can hinder supervised learning model accuracy. To address this issue, we propose a novel generation method that produces genuine banking graph models through a stochastic process. This process involves dividing the transaction history into distinct sections, which are connected randomly based on historical patterns, ensuring the resulting graphs accurately reflect real-world scenarios. By utilizing this graph model, we can train a supervised learning model to identify fraudulent transactions with higher precision. Moreover, our proposed graph model offers greater flexibility than existing methods, allowing for a higher degree of variation in transaction connections.

In X-ray binary systems involving black holes or neutron stars, a common process occurs when the compact object draws in material from a massive star, typically a white dwarf.  This material forms an accretion disc that can be observed as X-rays emitted from the system.  Another key phenomenon involves the massive star losing mass, which surrounds the compact object and contributes to accretion disc formation.  This mass loss has a significant impact on the system's evolution and the subsequent development of the accretion disc.  A recent study focused on the mass loss of single white dwarfs interacting with a compact object, specifically looking at mass loss rates and how they change over time.  The researchers used high-resolution computer simulations to study these interactions, which are influenced by the white dwarf's outer layer.  A range of mass loss rates were observed, from low to extremely high, and the findings suggest that these rates are determined by the stability of the white dwarf's surface layers.  High-resolution computer simulations of these interactions have provided new insights, which are discussed in the context of stellar evolution theory, showing that existing theories may need to be revised to better accommodate these results.

Future research at the JLC can provide valuable information about CP violation in weak interactions by examining rare processes such as $\tau$ decays into three-body final states. These studies will offer insights into final state interactions within hadronic systems and potentially uncover new CP-odd phases in the neutrino sector. To calculate cross sections and asymmetries for these decays, a novel framework combines the heavy baryon chiral Lagrangian with a three-body calculus, applying an iterative method to represent interaction terms as series of relativistic invariants. This report outlines the formulation of the framework and its application to $\tau$ decays, with specific findings for the direct and induced CP asymmetries in $\tau^{-} \to K^- K^ K^\nu_\tau$.

Ramsay and Wickelmaier (2002) introduced a family of models that use the symmetric Tversky ratio to combine multiple distances, syncing up discrete time points for multivariate functional data. These models, based on a categorization of data points across different dimensions, can treat data points as either identical, related, or distinct. We expand upon their work by deriving the maximum likelihood estimator for the parameterized space of metrics associated with these models. Notably, the extreme points of this space correspond to instances where multiple data points are considered identical or distinct. Notably, when data points are regarded as identical, the space of metrics remains unchanged, but this comes with a limitation: all identical labels must align at once, a constraint that can lead to biases in the resulting models. On the other hand, when data points are regarded as distinct, the space of metrics is fully expressive, but this comes with a cost: each distinct label must be assigned to a separate data point, a constraint that can lead to errors. To balance these biases and errors, we suggest combining identical and distinct labels through a process of group averaging. To achieve this, we first estimate the parameterized space of metrics using maximum likelihood, then project this estimate onto the space of all possible Tversky ratio-based metrics. The resulting hybrid model strikes a balance between the biases introduced by identical labels and the errors introduced by distinct labels. The feasibility and effectiveness of this hybrid model are illustrated through application to two real-world

In recent years, researchers have made significant advancements in single image deblurring techniques, achieving impressive results by integrating multiple methods. Despite these achievements, most existing models still face significant limitations in real-world applications due to the inability to account for the blurring process effectively. In this study, we address this limitation by developing a novel approach that incorporates a dedicated reblurring module within a hierarchical framework design. By reconstructing the sharp image feature map from the previous stage, the reblurring module enhances deblurring performance, while its inclusion enables the learning of blurring patterns, although in a reversed manner. The introduction of the reblurring module marks a notable shift in deblurring research, and our work offers a unique perspective on disentangling blurring and image generation. Moreover, our hierarchical framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of quantitative metrics, and produces visually appealing results that demonstrate its effectiveness in tackling real-world blurring applications.

We propose a novel approach to autonomous learning using chemical reaction networks (CRNs), drawing inspiration from the behavior of firing neurons. To achieve this, we develop a general framework for CRNs to represent autonomous agents navigating a grid world, interacting with their environment through input channels and output channels that modify their trajectory. The CRN is designed such that its species can be interpreted as the agent's mental state, and its reaction pathways are mapped to the underlying terrain features, allowing the agent to adapt through evolutionary processes. Furthermore, we demonstrate a method to modify this framework so that the CRN can learn to optimize a task by evolving species that correspond to cumulative reward values, along with reactions that adjust the agent's species according to those rewards.
